section: 4.2 What GDP Counts: Boundaries and Value Added
text:
4.2 What GDP Counts: Boundaries and Value Added

Conceptual Introduction
To measure aggregate output reliably without counting the same production twice, macroeconomists define Gross Domestic Product (GDP) strictly as the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country’s geographic borders during a specific time period. Every single phrase in that definition functions as an explicit accounting boundary rule:

Market Value: Physical quantities of apples, MRI scans, and commercial aircraft cannot be added directly in physical units. GDP converts diverse outputs into a common dollar metric by multiplying each good’s quantity by its market price (and includes imputed rental values for owner-occupied housing so homeownership and renting are treated consistently).
Final Goods and Services Only: A final good is sold to its end user (such as a laptop bought by a student), whereas an intermediate good is used up entirely in producing another good during the same period (such as a processor chip or sheet aluminum sold to a laptop manufacturer). Counting both the chip’s sale and the laptop’s retail price would double-count the chip. National accountants avoid double counting either by counting only final sales or by summing each firm’s value added—the market value of a firm’s output minus the cost of intermediate inputs purchased from other firms.
Within Domestic Borders: GDP is strictly geographic. A Toyota vehicle assembled in Georgetown, Kentucky counts toward U.S. GDP regardless of Japanese corporate ownership, whereas a Ford vehicle assembled in Hermosillo, Mexico counts toward Mexican GDP.
Current Production Only: GDP measures new production created during the current quarter or year. It excludes sales of used cars and existing homes (already counted when originally built), pure financial transactions such as buying stocks or bonds, and government transfer payments such as Social Security checks (which redistribute existing income rather than purchasing newly produced output).



Visual Representation
Figure 2 illustrates a three-stage laptop supply chain—from silicon wafer fabrication to CPU processor manufacturing to final retail assembly—demonstrating why summing value added across stages equals the final market price without double counting.



Figure 2. Value-Added Accounting Eliminates Double Counting. Summing gross sales across all three firms (\(\$100 + \$350 + \$1{,}000 = \$1{,}450\)) would count intermediate components twice; summing each stage’s value added matches the \(\$1{,}000\) final retail price.








NoteClear It Up: Four Classic GDP Boundary Pitfalls




Financial Investment vs. Economic Investment (\(I\)): Buying \(\$10{,}000\) of existing shares on the stock market transfers ownership of an existing financial claim; it does not create new goods and is excluded from GDP. Only newly built factories, machinery, software, new homes, and inventory additions count as \(I\).
Used Home Sales vs. Realtor Commissions: If a family buys a 20-year-old house for \(\$600{,}000\) and pays a real estate agent a \(\$30{,}000\) commission, the \(\$600{,}000\) house value is excluded (counted 20 years ago), while the \(\$30{,}000\) brokerage service is included because it represents current service production.
Domestic (GDP) vs. National (GNP): GDP counts output produced inside U.S. borders (even by foreign-owned firms), whereas Gross National Product (GNP) counts output produced by U.S.-owned factors anywhere in the world.
What GDP Leaves Out: GDP is a measure of market production, not total human well-being. It excludes unpaid household childcare, leisure time, underground cash transactions, and environmental degradation.





Mathematical Foundation
For any economy composed of \(n\) production stages or firms, firm \(i\)’s value added (\(VA_i\)) equals its gross sales revenue (\(R_i\)) minus the cost of intermediate inputs (\(IC_i\)) purchased from other firms:
\[
VA_i = R_i - IC_i, \qquad \text{GDP} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} VA_i = \text{Market Value of All Final Goods and Services}
\]
Trace a three-stage domestic supply chain (matching Figure 2):

Stage 1 (Silicon Wafer Supplier): Extracts raw quartz and produces a polished wafer with \(\$0\) purchased intermediate inputs, selling it to a chipmaker for \(\$100\). \[VA_1 = \$100 - \$0 = \$100\]
Stage 2 (CPU Processor Maker): Buys the \(\$100\) wafer and fabricates a processor chip, selling it to a laptop assembler for \(\$350\). \[VA_2 = \$350 - \$100 = \$250\]
Stage 3 (Laptop Assembler): Buys the \(\$350\) CPU (assuming no other purchased components for simplicity) and sells the finished laptop to a college student for \(\$1{,}000\). \[VA_3 = \$1{,}000 - \$350 = \$650\]
Verify Equivalence: \[\text{Total Value Added} = VA_1 + VA_2 + VA_3 = \$100 + \$250 + \$650 = \$1{,}000 = \text{Final Laptop Price}\] Summing gross receipts (\(\$100 + \$350 + \$1{,}000 = \$1{,}450\)) would overstate GDP by \(\$450\) because the wafer (\(\$100\)) was counted three times and the CPU fabrication (\(\$250\)) was counted twice.







TipReal-World Application: Global Semiconductor Supply Chains and Border Accounting



Consider a modern smartphone or AI server assembled in the United States using advanced logic chips fabricated in Taiwan, memory modules produced in South Korea, and assembly/software engineering performed domestically. Under BEA national accounting rules, only the value added created within U.S. borders enters U.S. GDP. When the U.S. assembler imports \(\$400\) of foreign chips and sells a finished server domestically for \(\$1{,}200\), the \(\$1{,}200\) sale appears in final domestic spending (\(C\) or \(I\)), while the \(\$400\) imported component is subtracted in net exports (\(-M\)), leaving exactly \(\$800\) of domestic U.S. value added recorded in U.S. GDP.

section: 4.3 Three Equivalent Accounting Views of the National Accounts
text:
4.3 Three Equivalent Accounting Views of the National Accounts

Conceptual Introduction
Every dollar spent by a buyer on a final good or service becomes a dollar of revenue for the producing firm, which in turn flows out as wages, rent, interest, or profit to the households and resource owners who supplied the inputs. Because every market transaction has both a buyer and a seller, the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) measures aggregate output through three mathematically equivalent approaches: the Expenditure Approach, the Production (Value-Added) Approach, and the Income Approach (Gross Domestic Income, GDI).
The Expenditure Approach adds up total spending on final domestic output across four macroeconomic sectors:

Personal Consumption Expenditures (\(C\)): Household spending on durable goods (cars, appliances), nondurable goods (groceries, gasoline), and services (healthcare, haircuts, housing rent).
Gross Private Domestic Investment (\(I\)): Business spending on new machinery, factories, and software (nonresidential fixed investment), newly constructed homes (residential fixed investment), and changes in business inventories (\(\Delta \text{Inventories}\)).
Government Consumption Expenditures and Gross Investment (\(G\)): Federal, state, and local government spending on final goods and services (public school teachers’ salaries, highway construction, defense equipment), strictly excluding transfer payments such as Social Security or unemployment insurance.
Net Exports (\(NX = X - M\)): Foreign spending on domestic exports (\(X\)) minus domestic spending on foreign imports (\(M\)). Imports are subtracted because \(C\), \(I\), and \(G\) record total domestic purchases regardless of where goods were made; subtracting \(M\) removes foreign-produced output so \(Y\) reflects domestic production only.

The Income Approach (Gross Domestic Income, GDI) sums all factor and non-factor incomes generated in producing domestic output: compensation of employees (wages, salaries, and benefits), proprietors’ income, rental income of persons, corporate profits, net interest, taxes on production and imports less subsidies, and consumption of fixed capital (depreciation). In theory, \(\text{GDP} \equiv \text{GDI}\) identically. In practice, because the BEA collects expenditure surveys and tax/payroll records from separate administrative sources with different reporting lags, measured GDP and measured GDI differ slightly; national accountants record this minor gap as the statistical discrepancy.


Visual Representation
Figure 3 maps the three-way NIPA accounting identity showing how Expenditure (\(C + I + G + NX\)), Production (Value Added), and Factor Income (GDI) measure the exact same circular flow of aggregate output.



Figure 3. Three-Way NIPA Equivalence. Expenditure (\(C + I + G + NX\)), Production (Value Added), and Factor Income (GDI) measure the exact same flow of current domestic production from three vantage points.




Mathematical Foundation
The fundamental national income accounting identity expresses aggregate output \(Y\) from both the expenditure and income sides:
\[
Y = C + I + G + (X - M)
\]
\[
\text{GDI} = \text{Compensation} + \text{Proprietors' Income} + \text{Rental Income} + \text{Corporate Profits} + \text{Net Interest} + (T_{\text{prod}} - \text{Sub}) + \delta K
\]
where \((T_{\text{prod}} - \text{Sub})\) denotes taxes on production and imports less subsidies, and \(\delta K\) denotes consumption of fixed capital (depreciation), with \(\text{GDP} = \text{GDI} + \text{Statistical Discrepancy}\).
Table~\(\ref{tab:nipa_worked}\) reports annual national account figures (in billions of dollars) for a hypothetical open economy. Note that the table includes two deliberate boundary distractors: Social Security transfer payments (\(\$1{,}400\text{B}\)) and existing home resales (\(\$950\text{B}\)).

Compute Net Exports (\(NX\)): \[NX = X - M = \$2{,}900\text{B} - \$3{,}600\text{B} = -\$700\text{ billion}\]
Compute GDP via the Expenditure Approach: Exclude Social Security transfers (\(\$1{,}400\text{B}\)) and used home resales (\(\$950\text{B}\)) because neither represents current production of final goods or services: \[\text{GDP} = C + I + G + NX = 16{,}500 + 4{,}400 + 4{,}600 + (-700) = \$24{,}800\text{ billion}\]
Verify via the Income Approach (GDI): Sum all factor incomes, indirect business taxes net of subsidies, and depreciation: \[\text{GDI} = 14{,}200 + 1{,}850 + 950 + 3{,}100 + 650 + 1{,}650 + 2{,}400 = \$24{,}800\text{ billion}\] Here, \(\text{GDP} = \text{GDI} = \$24{,}800\text{ billion}\) (zero statistical discrepancy).







TipReal-World Application: Why Economists Track Both GDP and GDI Around Turning Points



Although GDP and GDI must equal one another conceptually, their empirical quarterly releases from the BEA occasionally diverge by \(0.5\%\) to \(1.5\%\) because expenditure data come from retail, construction, and trade surveys while GDI comes from employer payroll tax filings and corporate profit reports. When the two series diverge near a potential recession, economists often average them together (published by the BEA as the ``Average of GDP and GDI’’) to filter out measurement noise and get a clearer real-time signal of whether hiring and output are slowing down.

title: 4  Chapter 4: Aggregate Output
section: 4.4 Nominal GDP vs. Real GDP
text:
4.4 Nominal GDP vs. Real GDP

Conceptual Introduction
Suppose an economy produces only coffee and laptops, and total dollar spending rises from \(\$10{,}000\) in Year 1 to \(\$14{,}000\) in Year 2. Does that \(40\%\) increase mean citizens actually enjoyed \(40\%\) more goods and services? Not necessarily. Because GDP measures market value (\(\text{Price} \times \text{Quantity}\)), total dollar spending can increase for two completely different reasons: (1) the economy produced more physical quantities of goods and services, or (2) firms charged higher market prices for the exact same quantities.
To disentangle physical output growth from price inflation, macroeconomists separate Nominal GDP from Real GDP:

Nominal GDP measures the value of current-period production evaluated at current-period market prices. Changes in Nominal GDP reflect both changes in physical quantities and changes in prices.
Real GDP measures the value of current-period production evaluated at constant base-year prices (or using a chain-type quantity index). By holding prices fixed at base-year levels, Real GDP eliminates price-level distortions so that any change in Real GDP reflects pure changes in physical output.

(Note: How economists use the ratio of Nominal GDP to Real GDP to construct economy-wide price indexes—specifically the GDP Implicit Price Deflator, alongside the Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index—is developed systematically in Chapter 5.)


Visual Representation
Figure 4 contrasts Nominal GDP against Base-Year Real GDP across two years for a simplified two-good economy (matching Work It Out 4.4), illustrating how rising prices inflate Nominal GDP growth (\(+40.0\%\)) far above true physical output growth (\(+12.0\%\)).



Figure 4. Separating Quantity Growth from Price Inflation. In the base year (Year 1), Nominal GDP equals Real GDP (\(\$10{,}000\)). In Year 2, Nominal GDP jumps \(40.0\%\) to \(\$14{,}000\), but holding prices constant reveals that physical Real GDP grew by \(12.0\%\) to \(\$11{,}200\).




Mathematical Foundation
For an economy producing \(k\) final goods indexed by \(j = 1, \dots, k\), let \(P_{j,t}\) and \(Q_{j,t}\) denote the price and quantity of good \(j\) in year \(t\), and let \(P_{j,0}\) denote the price of good \(j\) in the chosen base year (\(t = 0\)):
\[
\text{Nominal GDP}_t = \sum_{j=1}^{k} P_{j,t} \cdot Q_{j,t}, \qquad \text{Real GDP}_t = \sum_{j=1}^{k} P_{j,0} \cdot Q_{j,t}
\]
The annual percentage growth rate of Real GDP between year \(t-1\) and year \(t\) is:
\[
g_{Y,t} = \frac{\text{Real GDP}_t - \text{Real GDP}_{t-1}}{\text{Real GDP}_{t-1}} \times 100\%
\]
Consider a two-good economy producing Laptops and Coffee across two years, with Year 1 selected as the Base Year (Table~\(\ref{tab:nom_real_worked}\)).

Year 1 Nominal GDP and Real GDP (Base Year): In the base year, current prices equal base-year prices (\(P_1 = P_0\)), so Nominal GDP and Real GDP are identical: \[\text{Nominal GDP}_1 = (\$800 \times 10) + (\$4 \times 500) = \$8{,}000 + \$2{,}000 = \$10{,}000\] \[\text{Real GDP}_1 = (\$800 \times 10) + (\$4 \times 500) = \$10{,}000\]
Year 2 Nominal GDP (Current Year 2 Prices \(\times\) Year 2 Quantities): \[\text{Nominal GDP}_2 = (\$1{,}000 \times 11) + (\$5 \times 600) = \$11{,}000 + \$3{,}000 = \$14{,}000\] Nominal GDP rose by \(\frac{\$14{,}000 - \$10{,}000}{\$10{,}000} \times 100\% = +40.0\%\).
Year 2 Real GDP (Constant Year 1 Base Prices \(\times\) Year 2 Quantities): Holding prices fixed at Year 1 levels (\(\$800\) per laptop, \(\$4\) per cup): \[\text{Real GDP}_2 = (\$800 \times 11) + (\$4 \times 600) = \$8{,}800 + \$2{,}400 = \$11{,}200\]
Compute Real GDP Growth Rate and Price Effect: \[g_{Y,2} = \frac{\$11{,}200 - \$10{,}000}{\$10{,}000} \times 100\% = \frac{1{,}200}{10{,}000} \times 100\% = +12.0\%\] While Nominal GDP surged \(+40.0\%\) (by \(\$4{,}000\)), true physical output expanded by \(+12.0\%\) (\(\$1{,}200\) in base-year dollars). The remaining \(\$2{,}800\) gap (\(\$14{,}000 - \$11{,}200\)) reflects pure price inflation—resolving our opening Bring It Home puzzle.







TipReal-World Application: FRED Data—Current-Dollar (\texttt{GDP

Always measure economic growth rates and business cycle recessions using rather than . Furthermore, because chained-dollar levels reflect relative price weights anchored to the 2017 reference year, never interpret dollar levels as current-dollar spending.

Check Your Understanding

GDP Inclusion & Boundary Rules: Classify whether each transaction below is included in current-year U.S. GDP (and if so, under which expenditure component \(C, I, G,\) or \(NX\)) or excluded, explaining why in one sentence:
A household purchases a newly built townhouse from a residential developer for \(\$520{,}000\).
A retiree receives a \(\$2{,}100\) monthly Social Security payment from the federal government.
A domestic consumer buys a \(\$1{,}200\) smartphone assembled overseas and imported into the United States.
An automaker buys \(\$40{,}000\) of sheet steel from a domestic mill to stamp into new car doors sold later that same year.
Expenditure vs. Income Accounting: In a given year, an economy records \(C = \$12{,}400\text{B}\), \(I = \$3{,}200\text{B}\), \(G = \$3{,}800\text{B}\), \(X = \$2{,}100\text{B}\), and \(M = \$2{,}500\text{B}\).
Calculate Net Exports (\(NX\)) and total Expenditure GDP (\(Y\)).
If Compensation of Employees is \(\$11{,}100\text{B}\), Proprietors’ Income is \(\$1{,}400\text{B}\), Rental Income is \(\$700\text{B}\), Net Interest is \(\$500\text{B}\), Indirect Taxes Less Subsidies are \(\$1{,}300\text{B}\), and Depreciation is \(\$1{,}800\text{B}\), what must Corporate Profits equal if the statistical discrepancy is zero?
Nominal vs. Real GDP: Suppose an economy produces only electric bicycles. In Year 1 (Base Year), it produces \(1{,}000\) bikes at \(\$1{,}500\) each. In Year 2, it produces \(1{,}100\) bikes at \(\$1{,}800\) each.
Compute Nominal GDP in Year 1 and Year 2, and find the percentage change in Nominal GDP.
Compute Real GDP in Year 1 and Year 2 (using Year 1 base prices), and find the percentage growth rate of physical output.


Worked Solutions

(a) Included in \(I\): Newly constructed residential housing counts as gross private domestic investment (\(I\)). (b) Excluded: Social Security benefits are government transfer payments that redistribute income without purchasing current output. (c) Net zero effect on GDP: The \(\$1{,}200\) purchase adds \(+\$1{,}200\) to \(C\) and \(-\$1{,}200\) to \(NX\) (\(-M\)), leaving domestic GDP unchanged because the phone was produced abroad. (d) Excluded separately: Sheet steel is an intermediate good whose value is already embedded in the final retail price of the finished cars.
(a) \(NX = \$2{,}100\text{B} - \$2{,}500\text{B} = -\$400\text{ billion}\); \(Y = 12{,}400 + 3{,}200 + 3{,}800 + (-400) = \$19{,}000\text{ billion}\). (b) Summing known GDI items gives \(11{,}100 + 1{,}400 + 700 + 500 + 1{,}300 + 1{,}800 = \$16{,}800\text{B}\); with zero statistical discrepancy, Corporate Profits \(= \$19{,}000\text{B} - \$16{,}800\text{B} = \$2{,}200\text{ billion}\).
(a) \(\text{Nominal GDP}_1 = 1{,}000 \times \$1{,}500 = \$1{,}500{,}000\); \(\text{Nominal GDP}_2 = 1{,}100 \times \$1{,}800 = \$1{,}980{,}000\); percentage increase \(= \frac{1{,}980{,}000 - 1{,}500{,}000}{1{,}500{,}000} \times 100\% = +32.0\%\). (b) \(\text{Real GDP}_1 = \$1{,}500{,}000\); \(\text{Real GDP}_2 = 1{,}100 \times \$1{,}500 = \$1{,}650{,}000\); physical output growth \(= \frac{1{,}650{,}000 - 1{,}500{,}000}{1{,}500{,}000} \times 100\% = +10.0\%\).

TipBring It Home: Why a 4% Raise Can Leave You Poorer at the Grocery Store



Suppose you graduate, start a full-time job earning \(\$20.00\) per hour, and celebrate a year later when your manager awards you a \(4\%\) raise to \(\$20.80\) per hour. Your paycheck has eighty extra cents for every hour you work. Yet when you pay rent, buy groceries, and cover utilities, your bank balance feels tighter than it did a year earlier. How can a larger dollar paycheck buy fewer goods and services? The answer lies in distinguishing single-market nominal prices (studied in Chapter 3) from changes in the economy-wide aggregate price level. When broad consumer prices rise by \(5\%\) while your dollar wage rises by \(4\%\), your real purchasing power actually falls. Understanding how economists track the aggregate price level—and why both rapid inflation and outright deflation disrupt saving, borrowing, and wages—gives households and policymakers the tools needed to see past dollar illusions.

title: 5  Chapter 5: Inflation and Deflation
section: 5.1 Market Baskets, Price Indexes, and CPI Upward Biases
text:
5.1 Market Baskets, Price Indexes, and CPI Upward Biases

Conceptual Introduction
In Chapter 3, we analyzed how supply and demand determine the equilibrium price \(P^*\) of a single good, such as coffee or apartments. Across an entire macroeconomy, however, millions of individual prices rise and fall simultaneously at different speeds. To summarize whether the overall cost of living is rising or falling, economists construct a single summary statistic called the aggregate price level—an index number measuring the weighted average price of a standardized collection of goods and services relative to a chosen base period (where the index is normalized to \(100\)).
Because different economic groups buy and sell different bundles of goods, statistical agencies maintain three complementary price indexes. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), published monthly by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), tracks the retail cost of a fixed market basket of housing, food, transportation, medical care, energy, and apparel purchased by typical urban households—including imported consumer goods. The Producer Price Index (PPI) measures average wholesale selling prices received by domestic producers for raw materials, intermediate inputs, and finished goods; because producer input costs often pass through to retail shelves later, the PPI serves as an early warning indicator of consumer inflation. By contrast, the GDP Implicit Price Deflator (derived from the National Income and Product Accounts introduced in Chapter 4) measures price changes across all domestically produced final goods and services (\(C, I, G, X\)), excluding imports and updating its expenditure weights automatically every quarter.
These structural differences directly affect how households, businesses, and governments allocate resources. Social Security benefits, federal income tax brackets, and union wage contracts are indexed to the CPI, whereas macroeconomic growth adjustments rely on the GDP Deflator. Moreover, because the standard CPI holds base-period basket quantities fixed in the short run, it tends to overstate true increases in the cost of living—a systematic upward drift that affects public budget outlays and real wage measurements across the economy.


Visual Representation
Figure 1 compares the economic coverage, weighting structure, and import treatment across the three primary U.S. aggregate price indexes.



Figure 1. Comparing the Three Aggregate Price Indexes. The CPI tracks a fixed basket of urban consumer purchases (including imported consumer goods), the PPI tracks domestic wholesale producer prices, and the GDP Deflator covers all current domestically produced final goods and services (\(C, I, G, X\)).








NoteClear It Up: Why Does the CPI Overstate True Cost-of-Living Increases?



Because the standard CPI tracks the cost of purchasing a fixed basket of goods, economists estimate that it overstates true increases in the cost of living by roughly \(0.5\) to \(1.0\) percentage points per year due to three well-documented biases:

Substitution Bias: When the price of beef jumps while chicken stays cheap, households substitute toward chicken. A fixed-weight index assumes consumers keep buying the exact same expensive bundle, overstating the welfare loss.
Quality and New-Product Bias: When a new smartphone or laptop costs \(\$50\) more than last year’s model but delivers twice the battery life, camera resolution, and speed, part of the price tag reflects higher product quality rather than pure inflation. Similarly, brand-new inventions enter the fixed basket with a lag, missing steep early price declines.
Outlet Substitution Bias: Consumers shift purchases toward discount warehouse clubs and online retailers when retail prices rise, lowering actual prices paid relative to traditional store surveys.





Mathematical Foundation
To construct a fixed-basket price index such as the CPI, multiply the fixed base-period quantities (\(Q_{j,0}\)) of each item \(j = 1, \dots, k\) in the market basket by current-period prices (\(P_{j,t}\)), divide by the base-period cost of that identical basket, and multiply by \(100\):
\[
\text{Cost of Market Basket}_t = \sum_{j=1}^{k} P_{j,t} \cdot Q_{j,0}, \qquad
\text{CPI}_t = \frac{\text{Cost of Market Basket}_t}{\text{Cost of Market Basket}_0} \times 100.
\]
By construction, in the base period (\(t = 0\)), \(\text{CPI}_0 = \frac{\text{Cost}_0}{\text{Cost}_0} \times 100 = 100.0\). By contrast, the GDP Implicit Price Deflator uses current-period quantities (\(Q_{j,t}\)) and equals the ratio of Nominal GDP to Real GDP multiplied by \(100\):
\[
\text{GDP Deflator}_t = \frac{\text{Nominal GDP}_t}{\text{Real GDP}_t} \times 100 = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k} P_{j,t} \cdot Q_{j,t}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k} P_{j,0} \cdot Q_{j,t}} \times 100.
\]
Suppose an urban household market basket consists of \(10\) units of housing/utilities and \(50\) units of groceries. In the base year (\(t = 0\)), housing costs \(\$30\) per unit and groceries cost \(\$4\) per unit.

Compute the Base-Year Market Basket Cost (\(t = 0\)): \[\text{Cost of Market Basket}_0 = (\$30 \times 10) + (\$4 \times 50) = \$300 + \$200 = \$500\] \[\text{CPI}_0 = \frac{\$500}{\$500} \times 100 = 100.0\]
Compute Year 1 CPI when Basket Cost Rises to \(\$550\): Suppose in Year 1 (\(t = 1\)), housing rises to \(\$33\) per unit and groceries rise to \(\$4.40\) per unit, bringing the fixed-basket cost to \((\$33 \times 10) + (\$4.40 \times 50) = \$330 + \$220 = \$550\): \[\text{CPI}_1 = \frac{\$550}{\$500} \times 100 = 110.0\]
Compute Year 2 CPI when Basket Cost Falls to \(\$539\): Suppose in Year 2 (\(t = 2\)), lower energy and food prices reduce the basket cost to \(\$539\): \[\text{CPI}_2 = \frac{\$539}{\$500} \times 100 = 107.8\]
Compare with a GDP Deflator Calculation: Separately, if an economy produces Nominal GDP of \(\$27{,}500\text{ billion}\) and Real GDP of \(\$25{,}000\text{ billion}\) in Year 1, its GDP Implicit Price Deflator is: \[\text{GDP Deflator}_1 = \frac{\$27{,}500\text{B}}{\$25{,}000\text{B}} \times 100 = 110.0\]







TipFRED Data: Tracking Consumer and Producer Price Indexes (\texttt{CPIAUCSL



and )} In empirical macroeconomic analysis using Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED), two canonical monthly series anchor price-level monitoring:

: Reports the Producer Price Index by Commodity: All Commodities, indexed to \(1982 = 100\).

During the 2021–2022 global supply-chain bottleneck and energy surge, accelerated sharply several months before peaked, illustrating how wholesale commodity and freight price increases propagate along supply chains into retail consumer prices. Conversely, when imported consumer electronics or foreign crude oil fall in price, registers the relief directly because consumer imports sit inside the urban household basket, whereas the GDP Deflator excludes imported goods.

title: 5  Chapter 5: Inflation and Deflation
section: 5.2 Calculating National Inflation, Disinflation, and Deflation
text:
5.2 Calculating National Inflation, Disinflation, and Deflation

Conceptual Introduction
Once economists have an aggregate price index series (\(P_0, P_1, P_2, \dots\)), they measure the speed of economy-wide price changes through the inflation rate (\(\pi_t\))—the percentage rate of change in the aggregate price level from one period (\(t-1\)) to the next (\(t\)). Notice the crucial distinction between the price level (an index number such as \(\text{CPI} = 110.0\) or \(315.0\)) and the inflation rate (a percentage growth rate per year, such as \(+10.0\%\) or \(+3.2\%\)).
Economists classify aggregate price dynamics into three distinct regimes based on the sign and trajectory of \(\pi_t\):

Inflation (\(\pi_t > 0\)): A sustained increase in the aggregate price level, which erodes the purchasing power of each dollar.
Disinflation (\(\pi_t > 0\), with \(\pi_t < \pi_{t-1}\)): A slowdown in the rate of inflation—for example, annual inflation cooling from \(6.0\%\) to \(3.0\%\). During disinflation, the aggregate price level is still rising, just at a slower pace than before.
Deflation (\(\pi_t < 0\)): An outright decline in the aggregate price level, meaning average prices fall below their prior-period levels and the inflation rate turns negative.

Both high inflation and outright deflation distort economic decision-making and resource allocation. High, volatile inflation obscures relative price signals (making it hard for firms and shoppers to tell whether a price hike reflects higher demand or general inflation) and imposes real resource costs. Conversely, economy-wide deflation is dangerous because wages and debt contracts are denominated in fixed nominal dollars: falling prices raise the real burden of household and corporate debt, prompting borrowers to slash spending and firms to freeze hiring—a self-reinforcing contractionary spiral known as debt deflation.


Visual Representation
Figure 2 plots the hypothetical market-basket CPI trajectory from Work It Out 5.1 alongside a multi-period inflation rate path, visually separating rising prices during inflation and disinflation from falling prices during deflation.



Figure 2. Aggregate Price Levels vs. Inflation Regimes. Left: An index rise from \(100.0\) to \(110.0\) corresponds to \(+10.0\%\) inflation, whereas a drop from \(110.0\) to \(107.8\) corresponds to \(-2.0\%\) deflation. Right: Disinflation occurs when \(\pi_t\) declines toward \(0\%\) while remaining positive.








NoteClear It Up: Disinflation Is Not Deflation



Students frequently confuse disinflation with deflation when reading economic news. If headline CPI inflation falls from \(6.0\%\) in Year 1 to \(3.0\%\) in Year 2, the economy is experiencing disinflation, not deflation: average consumer prices still increased by \(3.0\%\) over Year 2, so the price index is higher than ever—it simply climbed less rapidly than in Year 1. Average prices fall below prior levels only when \(\pi_t < 0\) (deflation).




Mathematical Foundation
Let \(P_t\) denote the value of an aggregate price index (such as the CPI or GDP Deflator) in period \(t\), and let \(P_{t-1}\) denote its value in the immediately preceding period. The percentage inflation rate \(\pi_t\) is:
\[
\pi_t = \frac{P_t - P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}} \times 100\% = \left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}} - 1\right) \times 100\%.
\]
Notice that the denominator is always the prior period’s index (\(P_{t-1}\)), not the base-year index (\(100.0\)), unless \(t - 1\) happens to be the base year.
Using the market-basket CPI series from Work It Out 5.1—where the basket costs \(\$500\) in Year 0 (\(t = 0\)), \(\$550\) in Year 1 (\(t = 1\)), and \(\$539\) in Year 2 (\(t = 2\))—compute the annual inflation rate for each year:

Year 1 Inflation Rate (\(\pi_1\), from Year 0 to Year 1): With \(\text{CPI}_0 = 100.0\) and \(\text{CPI}_1 = 110.0\): \[\pi_1 = \frac{\text{CPI}_1 - \text{CPI}_0}{\text{CPI}_0} \times 100\% = \frac{110.0 - 100.0}{100.0} \times 100\% = \frac{10.0}{100.0} \times 100\% = +10.0\%.\] Because \(\pi_1 > 0\), the economy experiences inflation of \(10.0\%\).
Year 2 Inflation Rate (\(\pi_2\), from Year 1 to Year 2): With \(\text{CPI}_1 = 110.0\) and \(\text{CPI}_2 = 107.8\): \[\pi_2 = \frac{\text{CPI}_2 - \text{CPI}_1}{\text{CPI}_1} \times 100\% = \frac{107.8 - 110.0}{110.0} \times 100\% = \frac{-2.2}{110.0} \times 100\% = -2.0\%.\] Because \(\pi_2 < 0\), the economy experiences outright deflation of \(2.0\%\). (Note: A common algebra error is dividing \(-2.2\) by the Year 0 base index \(100.0\) instead of Year 1’s index \(110.0\), which would falsely yield \(-2.2\%\).)
Contrast with a Disinflation Scenario: If instead the Year 2 basket cost had risen to \(\$577.50\) (\(\text{CPI}_2 = \frac{577.50}{500} \times 100 = 115.5\)), then: \[\pi_2^{\text{alt}} = \frac{115.5 - 110.0}{110.0} \times 100\% = \frac{5.5}{110.0} \times 100\% = +5.0\%.\] Here \(\pi_2^{\text{alt}} = +5.0\% < \pi_1 = +10.0\%\), representing disinflation (inflation slowed by \(5.0\) percentage points, even though prices still rose \(5.0\%\)).







TipU.S. Post-Pandemic Disinflation (2022–2024) vs. Japan’s Lost Decades of Deflation



Between 2021 and mid-2022, U.S. year-over-year CPI inflation () surged above \(8\%\), driven by pandemic supply-chain disruptions, fiscal stimulus, and energy price shocks. Over 2023 and 2024, tighter monetary policy and healing supply chains brought annual U.S. inflation back down toward \(3\%\)—a textbook episode of disinflation in which the price level stabilized at a higher plateau rather than returning to 2019 prices. By contrast, following the burst of its asset-price bubble in the early 1990s, Japan experienced prolonged deflation (\(\pi_t < 0\)) across much of the late 1990s and 2000s. Expecting prices to be even lower next year, Japanese households postponed durable purchases and corporations delayed capital investment, illustrating why central banks target a low, positive inflation rate (typically \(2\%\)) rather than \(0\%\) or negative inflation.

title: 5  Chapter 5: Inflation and Deflation
section: 5.3 Real Purchasing Power, Indexation, and Costs of Inflation
text:
5.3 Real Purchasing Power, Indexation, and Costs of Inflation

Conceptual Introduction
Because dollars are merely measuring rods whose purchasing power shrinks during inflation, economists separate nominal variables (measured in current-period dollars, such as a \(\$20.80\) hourly wage) from real variables (adjusted for changes in the aggregate price level to measure actual purchasing power over physical goods and services). If every wage, pension, and price doubled overnight, real purchasing power would be unchanged—a property known as money neutrality in the long run.
In the short run, however, wages, tax thresholds, and contracts adjust unevenly, creating three distinct resource costs when inflation is elevated or unanticipated:

Shoe-Leather Costs: High inflation erodes the purchasing power of cash sitting in non-interest-bearing wallets or low-interest checking accounts, forcing households and firms to spend extra time and effort (“wearing out shoe leather”) making frequent trips to the bank or shifting funds between interest-bearing assets and cash.
Menu Costs: Businesses must spend real resources—printing new restaurant menus, re-tagging retail shelves, updating digital catalogs, and renegotiating supplier quotes—every time they adjust nominal prices.
Unit-of-Account Costs: Inflation makes the dollar a shrinking yardstick over time, distorting accounting profits, capital gains taxes, and long-term business planning. For example, if an asset rises \(10\%\) in nominal value solely because of \(10\%\) inflation, the investor earned zero real gain yet may still owe capital gains taxes on the illusory nominal profit.

To shield households from unintended purchasing-power erosion, governments and private contracts use automatic indexation—tying dollar payments directly to a published price index. For example, U.S. Social Security retirement benefits receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) tied to the Consumer Price Index, and federal income tax brackets are indexed annually to prevent bracket creep (being pushed into a higher marginal tax rate solely because nominal income rose with inflation).


Visual Representation
Figure 3 illustrates the hourly wage example from our chapter opening: although the worker’s nominal hourly wage rises \(+4.0\%\) from \(\$20.00\) to \(\$20.80\), consumer prices rise \(+5.0\%\) (\(\text{CPI}\) from \(300\) to \(315\)), reducing the worker’s real wage in base-period dollars from \(\$6.667\) to \(\$6.603\) (\(-0.95\%\)).



Figure 3. Nominal Wage Growth vs. Real Purchasing Power. Even though the worker’s nominal wage rises \(4.0\%\) (from \(\$20.00\) to \(\$20.80\)), a \(5.0\%\) jump in the CPI (from \(300\) to \(315\)) reduces real purchasing power by \(0.95\%\).




Mathematical Foundation
To convert any nominal dollar amount \(X_t^{\text{nom}}\) (such as a wage, salary, or historical price) into constant base-period purchasing power (\(X_t^{\text{real}}\)), divide by period \(t\)’s price index and multiply by \(100\):
\[
W_t^{\text{real}} = \frac{W_t^{\text{nom}}}{\text{CPI}_t} \times 100.
\]
More generally, to compare a dollar figure from historical period \(A\) in the purchasing power of target period \(B\):
\[
\text{Value in Period } B \text{ Dollars} = \text{Nominal Value}_A \times \frac{\text{CPI}_B}{\text{CPI}_A}.
\]
Suppose a worker’s nominal hourly wage rises from \(\$20.00\) in Period 0 to \(\$20.80\) in Period 1, while the CPI rises from \(300\) in Period 0 to \(315\) in Period 1.

Compute Nominal Wage Growth (\(g_W\)) and Inflation (\(\pi\)): \[g_W = \frac{\$20.80 - \$20.00}{\$20.00} \times 100\% = \frac{\$0.80}{\$20.00} \times 100\% = +4.0\%,\] \[\pi = \frac{315 - 300}{300} \times 100\% = \frac{15}{300} \times 100\% = +5.0\%.\]
Compute Real Wages in Constant Base-Period Dollars (\(\text{CPI}_{\text{base}} = 100\)): \[W_0^{\text{real}} = \frac{\$20.00}{300} \times 100 \approx \$6.667 \text{ per hour},\] \[W_1^{\text{real}} = \frac{\$20.80}{315} \times 100 \approx \$6.603 \text{ per hour}.\]
Compute the Percentage Change in Real Purchasing Power (retaining full precision): \[g_{\text{real}} = \frac{W_1^{\text{real}} - W_0^{\text{real}}}{W_0^{\text{real}}} \times 100\% = \left(\frac{20.80 / 315}{20.00 / 300} - 1\right) \times 100\% = \left(\frac{1.04}{1.05} - 1\right) \times 100\% \approx -0.95\%.\] Because nominal wage growth (\(+4.0\%\)) trailed CPI inflation (\(+5.0\%\)), the worker’s real hourly purchasing power declined by approximately \(0.95\%\).







TipSocial Security COLAs, Minimum Wage Erosion, and Historical Comparisons



Deflating nominal dollar values into constant-dollar purchasing power allows economists to compare living standards across decades or evaluate whether statutory benefits keep pace with inflation. For instance, if the federal minimum wage remains fixed at \(\$7.25\) per hour in nominal terms while the CPI rises over fifteen years, the real purchasing power of that statutory wage floor falls steadily every single year. Conversely, because Social Security benefits are legally indexed to the CPI, recipients receive an automatic annual Cost-of-Living Adjustment (such as the \(8.7\%\) COLA in 2023 following 2022 inflation) designed to preserve real purchasing power—though upward CPI substitution bias means full CPI indexation slightly overcompensates for true cost-of-living changes.

title: 5  Chapter 5: Inflation and Deflation
section: 5.4 Real vs. Nominal Interest Rates and the Fisher Equation
text:
5.4 Real vs. Nominal Interest Rates and the Fisher Equation

Conceptual Introduction
Just as workers care about how many groceries their wages can buy, savers and borrowers care about how much purchasing power a loan repays. When you deposit money in a savings account or take out a fixed-rate auto loan, the bank quotes a nominal interest rate (\(i\))—the annual percentage return measured in current dollars without adjusting for inflation. However, if prices rise while the loan is outstanding, the dollars repaid at maturity buy fewer goods than the dollars originally lent.
To measure the true gain in purchasing power earned by a lender (and the true real cost paid by a borrower), economist Irving Fisher established the distinction between the nominal interest rate (\(i\)) and the real interest rate (\(r\))—the nominal interest rate adjusted for inflation. Because inflation over the life of a loan is unknown at the moment a loan contract is signed, lenders and borrowers negotiate the nominal rate \(i\) based on their expected inflation rate (\(\pi^e\)), targeting a desired expected real return \(r^e = i - \pi^e\) (a relationship known as the Fisher Effect: higher expected inflation pushes nominal interest rates upward one-for-one).
Once the loan period concludes and actual inflation (\(\pi\)) is observed, the realized real interest rate is \(r_{\text{actual}} = i - \pi\). Whenever actual inflation differs from expected inflation, fixed-rate debt contracts arbitrarily redistribute real wealth between creditors and debtors:

Unexpectedly High Inflation (\(\pi > \pi^e\)): Realized real interest rates fall below expected real rates (\(r_{\text{actual}} < r^e\)). Borrowers win because they repay their fixed-dollar debts with cheaper, less valuable dollars; lenders lose purchasing power.
Unexpectedly Low Inflation or Deflation (\(\pi < \pi^e\)): Realized real interest rates rise above expected real rates (\(r_{\text{actual}} > r^e\)). Lenders win because repaid dollars buy more goods than anticipated; borrowers lose because the real burden of debt repayment increases.



Visual Representation
Figure 4 decomposes a \(7.0\%\) fixed nominal loan rate (\(i = 7.0\%\)) under \(3.0\%\) expected inflation (\(\pi^e = 3.0\%\), yielding \(r^e = 4.0\%\)) and contrasts what happens when actual inflation surges unexpectedly to \(\pi = 6.0\%\), compressing the lender’s realized real return to \(r_{\text{actual}} = 1.0\%\).



Figure 4. The Fisher Equation and Unexpected Inflation Redistribution. On a \(7.0\%\) fixed-rate loan priced for \(3.0\%\) expected inflation (\(r^e = 4.0\%\)), an unexpected inflation surge to \(6.0\%\) transfers \(3.0\) percentage points of real purchasing power from the lender to the borrower (\(r_{\text{actual}} = 1.0\%\)).








NoteClear It Up: Can the Real Interest Rate Be Negative?



Yes. While nominal interest rates on ordinary bank loans and deposits rarely fall below zero (because savers can hold physical currency yielding \(0\%\)), the real interest rate (\(r = i - \pi\)) turns negative whenever inflation exceeds the nominal interest rate (\(\pi > i\)). For example, if a savings account pays \(i = 2.0\%\) nominal interest while consumer prices rise by \(\pi = 5.0\%\), your account balance grows by \(2.0\%\) in dollars, but those dollars buy \(3.0\%\) fewer goods (\(r \approx 2.0\% - 5.0\% = -3.0\%\)).




Mathematical Foundation
For moderate inflation and interest rates, the linear Fisher Equation relates the nominal interest rate (\(i\)), expected or realized real interest rate (\(r\)), and expected or actual inflation rate (\(\pi^e\) or \(\pi\)):
\[
i = r^e + \pi^e \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad r^e = i - \pi^e \quad (\text{expected}), \qquad r_{\text{actual}} = i - \pi \quad (\text{realized}).
\]
A credit union and a small business agree on a one-year fixed-rate loan of \(\$10{,}000\) at a nominal interest rate of \(i = 7.0\%\). At the time the contract is signed, both parties expect annual inflation to be \(\pi^e = 3.0\%\).

Compute the Expected Real Interest Rate (\(r^e\)): \[r^e = i - \pi^e = 7.0\% - 3.0\% = 4.0\%.\] Both lender and borrower anticipate that the credit union will gain \(4.0\%\) in real purchasing power over the year.
Compute the Realized Real Interest Rate (\(r_{\text{actual}}\)) if Actual Inflation Hits \(\pi = 6.0\%\): \[r_{\text{actual}} = i - \pi = 7.0\% - 6.0\% = 1.0\%.\]
Identify Who Gained and Who Lost from the Inflation Surprise: Because actual inflation (\(\pi = 6.0\%\)) exceeded expected inflation (\(\pi^e = 3.0\%\)) by \(3.0\) percentage points, the lender’s realized real return fell from \(4.0\%\) to \(1.0\%\), transferring \(3.0\%\) of real purchasing power (\(\$300\) on a \(\$10{,}000\) loan) from the credit union to the small-business borrower.
Compute the Realized Real Interest Rate if Unexpected Disinflation Drops \(\pi\) to \(1.0\%\): \[r_{\text{actual}}^{\text{low}} = 7.0\% - 1.0\% = 6.0\%.\] Here realized inflation was \(2.0\) percentage points lower than expected, raising the lender’s real return to \(6.0\%\) and hurting the borrower.







TipFixed-Rate Mortgages and Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS)



In the United States, millions of homeowners hold \(30\)-year fixed-rate mortgages locked in at nominal rates between \(3.0\%\) and \(4.0\%\) during 2020–2021. When U.S. inflation subsequently exceeded \(4\%\) to \(8\%\) in 2021–2023, those borrowers experienced negative realized real mortgage rates (\(r_{\text{actual}} = i - \pi < 0\)), substantially reducing the real purchasing-power burden of their monthly mortgage payments while eroding the real returns of mortgage bondholders. To protect savers against unexpected inflation, the U.S. Treasury issues Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), whose principal value adjusts automatically with the CPI (), guaranteeing investors a fixed real return regardless of future inflation surprises.

Check Your Understanding

Price Index Coverage & Biases:
Suppose the price of imported European olive oil and imported Japanese automobiles jumps sharply, while prices of all domestically produced U.S. goods stay constant. Which index rises more: the U.S. CPI or the U.S. GDP Implicit Price Deflator? Explain why in one sentence.
Explain how substitution bias and quality/new-product bias cause a fixed-basket CPI to overstate true cost-of-living increases.
Inflation, Disinflation, and Deflation: Suppose an economy’s CPI is \(200.0\) in Year 1, \(216.0\) in Year 2, \(222.48\) in Year 3, and \(218.03\) in Year 4.
Calculate the annual inflation rate for Year 2, Year 3, and Year 4.
Classify each year (Year 2, Year 3, Year 4) as experiencing inflation, disinflation, or deflation.
Real Wages and the Fisher Equation:
A worker’s nominal hourly wage rises by \(3.0\%\) while CPI inflation is \(6.0\%\). Use the exact multiplicative relation \(1 + g_{\text{real}} = \frac{1 + g_W}{1 + \pi}\) to compute exact real wage growth.
A bank issues a fixed-rate loan at a nominal interest rate of \(i = 6.5\%\) when expected inflation is \(\pi^e = 2.5\%\). What is the expected real interest rate \(r^e\)? If actual inflation turns out to be \(\pi = 5.0\%\), what is the realized real interest rate \(r_{\text{actual}}\), and who benefits from the surprise?


Worked Solutions

(a) U.S. CPI rises more: The CPI tracks a basket of urban consumer purchases that includes imported consumer goods, whereas the GDP Deflator measures only domestically produced final goods and services (\(C, I, G, X\)) and excludes imports. (b) Substitution bias occurs because fixed base-year weights ignore consumers switching away from items whose relative prices rise fastest; quality/new-product bias occurs because fixed-basket surveys treat higher prices for improved technology/quality as pure price inflation and incorporate new products after their initial steep price drops.
(a) Year 2: \(\pi_2 = \frac{216.0 - 200.0}{200.0} \times 100\% = +8.0\%\); Year 3: \(\pi_3 = \frac{222.48 - 216.0}{216.0} \times 100\% = +3.0\%\); Year 4: \(\pi_4 = \frac{218.03 - 222.48}{222.48} \times 100\% \approx -2.0\%\). (b) Year 2 experiences inflation (\(+8.0\%\)); Year 3 experiences disinflation (\(+3.0\% < +8.0\%\), prices still rising but more slowly); Year 4 experiences deflation (\(-2.0\% < 0\)).
(a) \(1 + g_{\text{real}} = \frac{1.03}{1.06} \approx 0.9717 \implies g_{\text{real}} \approx -2.83\%\) (real purchasing power falls by \(2.83\%\)). (b) Expected real interest rate: \(r^e = 6.5\% - 2.5\% = 4.0\%\). Realized real interest rate: \(r_{\text{actual}} = 6.5\% - 5.0\% = 1.5\%\) (or exact: \(\frac{0.065 - 0.05}{1.05} \approx 1.43\%\)). Because actual inflation (\(5.0\%\)) exceeded expected inflation (\(2.5\%\)), the borrower benefits at the expense of the lender.

title: 6  Ch06 Unemployment
6  Ch06 Unemployment
text:
Conceptual Introduction
Assessing the health of the macroeconomy requires measuring not only how much output an economy produces, but also how effectively it utilizes its human resources. In the United States, official labor market statistics derive primarily from the Current Population Survey (CPS), a monthly household survey of roughly \(60{,}000\) eligible households conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau for the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Rather than asking whether a respondent feels employed or desires a job, the CPS classifies individuals through a strict, hierarchical sequence of behavioral questions covering a specific reference week (usually the calendar week containing the 12th day of the month). This objective behavioral standard ensures consistent measurement across business cycles and demographic groups.
The survey begins with the Civilian Noninstitutional Population (\(P\) or \(\text{CNIP}\)), which encompasses all U.S. residents aged 16 and older who are not serving on active duty in the Armed Forces and are not residing in institutions such as correctional facilities, nursing homes, or residential psychiatric hospitals. Within this base population, respondents are partitioned into three mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive categories: Employed (\(E\)), Unemployed (\(U\)), and Not in the Labor Force (\(\text{NILF}\)).
To be counted as employed (\(E\)), an individual must have worked at least one hour for pay or profit during the reference week, worked at least 15 unpaid hours in a family-operated enterprise, or held a job from which they were temporarily absent due to illness, vacation, weather, industrial dispute, or parental leave. To be counted as unemployed (\(U\)), a person must simultaneously satisfy three conditions: (1) have no employment during the reference week, (2) be currently available to start work (except for temporary illness), and (3) have engaged in active job search—such as submitting applications, interviewing, contacting employers, or answering job advertisements—within the preceding four weeks. Workers on temporary layoff awaiting recall are also counted in \(U\) even without active search. Anyone in the civilian noninstitutional population who is neither employed nor actively searching is classified as not in the labor force (\(\text{NILF}\)), including full-time students, retirees, homemakers, and individuals who have stopped looking for work.
Alongside the CPS household survey, the BLS conducts the Current Employment Statistics (CES) Establishment Survey, which samples roughly \(122{,}000\) businesses and government agencies covering approximately \(666{,}000\) worksites. While the CPS measures the unemployment rate and demographic labor force status by surveying households (counting self-employed, agricultural, and unpaid family workers), the CES measures nonfarm payroll employment, average weekly hours, and average hourly earnings by surveying employer payrolls. Because a worker holding two jobs appears once in CPS employment (\(E\)) but twice on CES establishment payrolls, the two surveys provide complementary lenses on labor market momentum.


Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates the hierarchical BLS classification tree applied to our flagship benchmark economy, where the Civilian Noninstitutional Population equals \(200.0\text{ million}\). Notice how the labor force (\(120.0\text{ million}\)) forms the core active market, while \(\text{NILF}\) (\(80.0\text{ million}\)) contains critical subgroups—specifically marginally attached and discouraged workers—that lie on the boundary of labor market participation.



Figure 1. BLS Household Survey Population Partition and Flagship Quantitative Baseline.




Mathematical Foundation
Let \(P\) denote the Civilian Noninstitutional Population, \(E\) total employment, \(U\) total unemployment, and \(\text{NILF}\) those not in the labor force. The fundamental population accounting identities are: \[\begin{align}
\text{LF} &= E + U \label{eq:lf_identity} \\
P &= \text{LF} + \text{NILF} = E + U + \text{NILF} \label{eq:cnip_identity}
\end{align}\] From these aggregates, three core headline labor market rates are defined: \[\begin{align}
\text{Headline Unemployment Rate (U-3)} &= \frac{U}{\text{LF}} \times 100 = \frac{U}{E + U} \times 100 \label{eq:u3} \\
\text{Labor Force Participation Rate (LFPR)} &= \frac{\text{LF}}{P} \times 100 = \frac{E + U}{P} \times 100 \label{eq:lfpr} \\
\text{Employment-to-Population Ratio (EPOP)} &= \frac{E}{P} \times 100 \label{eq:epop}
\end{align}\] Notice that when expressed as proportions, these three indicators are algebraically linked through the identity \(\text{EPOP} = \text{LFPR} \times (1 - \text{U-3})\).
Flagship Baseline Calculation. Using our benchmark economy (\(P = 200.0\text{M}\), \(E = 114.0\text{M}\), \(U = 6.0\text{M}\), and \(\text{NILF} = 80.0\text{M}\)):
\[
\text{LF} = 114.0 + 6.0 = 120.0\text{M}
\]
\[
\text{U-3} = \frac{6.0}{120.0} \times 100 = 5.00\%, \qquad
\text{LFPR} = \frac{120.0}{200.0} \times 100 = 60.00\%, \qquad
\text{EPOP} = \frac{114.0}{200.0} \times 100 = 57.00\%
\]






NoteClear It Up: Why Discouraged Workers Lower the Headline Unemployment Rate



A common misconception is that when an unemployed worker gives up searching for a job out of frustration, the headline unemployment rate rises. In fact, the exact opposite occurs. Because an individual must actively search within the past four weeks to remain in \(U\), ceasing job search moves the worker out of both the numerator (\(U\)) and the denominator (\(\text{LF} = E + U\)) of \(\text{U-3} = U / \text{LF}\). Since \(U < \text{LF}\), subtracting the same positive number from both numerator and denominator strictly reduces the fraction. Thus, a wave of discouragement during a prolonged recession artificially depresses the headline unemployment rate even though labor market conditions have deteriorated.




Real-World Application
Tracking both the headline unemployment rate () and participation indicators in the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) repository reveals structural shifts that the unemployment rate alone cannot capture. Specifically, macroeconomists pair with two demographic engagement ratios: the Labor Force Participation Rate () and the Employment-to-Population Ratio ().
Between 2000 and 2015, the U.S. declined steadily from roughly \(67.3\%\) to \(62.4\%\), driven primarily by the aging of the Baby Boom cohort into retirement alongside lower participation among younger workers pursuing higher education. During the onset of the COVID-19 shock in spring 2020, plunged by roughly \(3\) percentage points as lockdowns prevented millions of displaced workers from conducting active job searches, temporarily classifying them as \(\text{NILF}\) rather than unemployed. Consequently, economists monitor —the share of the entire working-age population actively holding a job—as well as Prime-Age EPOP (ages 25–54, ) as robust cross-checks that strip out population aging and shifts between \(U\) and \(\text{NILF}\).

title: 6  Ch06 Unemployment
section: 6.2 Measuring Underutilization: Headline U-3 vs. Broad U-6
text:
6.2 Measuring Underutilization: Headline U-3 vs. Broad U-6

Conceptual Introduction
While the headline U-3 rate serves as the standard benchmark for joblessness, it treats employment as a binary state: working just one hour per week for pay places a person in \(E\), regardless of whether they seek a full-time career. Similarly, U-3 excludes individuals on the periphery of the labor market who want to work and have searched recently, even if they did not search during the specific four-week CPS window. During economic downturns, firms often cut employee hours before laying off staff (intensive-margin adjustment), while long-term jobless workers temporarily pause active applications. Relying solely on U-3 therefore understates total labor slack.
To capture hidden underemployment and latent labor supply, the BLS publishes six alternative measures of labor underutilization, labeled U-1 through U-6. As summarized in Table~\(\ref{tab:bls_u1_u6}\), these measures progress systematically from narrow indicators of long-term joblessness (U-1) and job losers (U-2) to the official headline rate (U-3), and finally to broad measures incorporating discouraged workers (U-4), all marginally attached workers (U-5), and involuntary part-time workers (U-6).
The broadest measure, U-6, expands U-3 by incorporating two critical groups: [leftmargin=1.5em, itemsep=3pt] * Marginally Attached Workers (\(M\)): Persons currently classified as \(\text{NILF}\) who want and are available for a job and have actively looked for work sometime in the past 12 months, though not in the past four weeks. A key subset of \(M\) is Discouraged Workers (\(D\)), who cite labor-market reasons—such as believing no jobs are available in their line of work or lacking required schooling—for not searching recently. Other marginally attached workers cite non-market barriers such as childcare or transportation constraints. * Persons Employed Part-Time for Economic Reasons (\(PT_{\text{econ}}\)): Also termed involuntary part-time workers, these are individuals working fewer than 35 hours per week who prefer full-time employment and are available for full-time hours, but whose hours were reduced due to slack business conditions or inability to find a full-time position.


Visual Representation
Figure 2 contrasts the composition of U-3 and U-6 in our flagship baseline economy. Moving from U-3 to U-6 expands the numerator from \(6.0\text{M}\) to \(14.0\text{M}\) by adding marginally attached workers (\(3.0\text{M}\)) and involuntary part-time workers (\(5.0\text{M}\)). Because marginally attached workers are drawn from \(\text{NILF}\), they must simultaneously be added to the denominator so that the rate remains a consistent proportion of the expanded labor pool (\(\text{LF} + M = 123.0\text{M}\)).



Figure 2. Decomposition of Numerators, Denominators, and Rates for U-3 versus U-6.




Mathematical Foundation
Formally, let \(M\) denote all marginally attached workers (with \(D \subseteq M\) representing discouraged workers) and let \(PT_{\text{econ}}\) denote persons employed part-time for economic reasons. The broad underutilization rate U-6 is defined as:
\[
\text{U-6} = \frac{U + M + PT_{\text{econ}}}{\text{LF} + M} \times 100
\label{eq:u6}
\]
Notice why \(PT_{\text{econ}}\) is added only to the numerator whereas \(M\) is added to both numerator and denominator: [leftmargin=1.5em, itemsep=2pt] * \(PT_{\text{econ}}\) workers are already employed (\(PT_{\text{econ}} \subset E \subset \text{LF}\)), so they are already counted inside \(\text{LF}\) in the denominator. * \(M\) workers are classified as \(\text{NILF}\) (\(M \subset \text{NILF}\)), so they are excluded from \(\text{LF}\) and must be added to the denominator so that U-6 remains bounded between \(0\%\) and \(100\%\).
Flagship Baseline Calculation. Using \(U = 6.0\text{M}\), \(\text{LF} = 120.0\text{M}\), \(M = 3.0\text{M}\) (of which \(D = 1.2\text{M}\) are discouraged), and \(PT_{\text{econ}} = 5.0\text{M}\):
\[
\text{U-6} = \frac{6.0 + 3.0 + 5.0}{120.0 + 3.0} \times 100 = \frac{14.0}{123.0} \times 100 \approx 11.38\%
\]
The underutilization spread in the baseline economy is \(\text{U-6} - \text{U-3} = 11.38\% - 5.00\% = 6.38\text{ percentage points}\).


Real-World Application
The spread between U-6 () and U-3 () acts as a sensitive barometer of labor-market intensity and work-hour rationing. Following the 2007–2009 Great Recession, U-3 peaked at \(10.0\%\) in October 2009, while U-6 surged to \(17.1\%\)—a spread of \(7.1\) percentage points—reflecting millions of retail, construction, and service employees whose schedules were cut to part-time and a historic wave of long-term discouraged workers. By contrast, during the tight labor market of 2022–2023, U-3 fell to \(3.4\%\) and U-6 dropped to \(6.5\%\), compressing the spread to just \(3.1\) percentage points as firms converted part-time roles into full-time schedules to retain staff.
In modern labor markets featuring flexible scheduling and independent platform work, involuntary part-time employment remains structurally sensitive to aggregate demand. Note a critical classification rule: workers who choose part-time schedules voluntarily—such as students, semi-retirees, or caregivers preferring 20 hours per week—are classified as part-time for noneconomic reasons and are not included in \(PT_{\text{econ}}\) or U-6. Likewise, because discouraged workers (\(D\)) are already a subset of marginally attached workers (\(M\)), adding both \(M\) and \(D\) into the U-6 numerator would double-count discouraged workers.

title: 6  Ch06 Unemployment
section: 6.3 Types of Unemployment, Institutional Rigidities, and the Natural Rate (\(u^*\))
text:
6.3 Types of Unemployment, Institutional Rigidities, and the Natural Rate (\(u^*\))

Conceptual Introduction
Even in a booming economy operating at full capacity, the unemployment rate never falls to zero. Economists decompose observed unemployment (\(u\)) into three distinct components based on underlying economic causes: [leftmargin=1.5em, itemsep=3pt] * Frictional Unemployment (\(u_f\)): Short-term unemployment arising from the normal process of matching heterogeneous workers with heterogeneous job openings. Imperfect information, geographic mobility, recent graduation, and career transitions mean that workers and firms require time to search, interview, and negotiate offers. Frictional unemployment is largely voluntary and efficiency-enhancing because better matches raise long-run productivity. * Structural Unemployment (\(u_s\)): Persistent unemployment resulting from a mismatch between the skills, occupational credentials, or geographic locations of job seekers and the requirements of available vacancies, or from institutional wage rigidities that hold real wages above the market-clearing equilibrium. Unlike frictional search, structurally unemployed workers face a genuine shortage of jobs at prevailing wages. * Cyclical Unemployment (\(u_c\)): The deviation of actual unemployment from the economy’s long-run sustainable benchmark, driven by short-run fluctuations in aggregate demand across the business cycle. During recessions, falling aggregate spending reduces labor demand across industries (\(u_c > 0\)); during economic expansions, tight labor markets push actual unemployment below its normal level (\(u_c < 0\)).
The sum of frictional and structural unemployment defines the Natural Rate of Unemployment (\(u^*\)), also referred to in monetary policy analysis as the Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU). When \(u = u^*\), cyclical unemployment is zero (\(u_c = 0\)) and the economy is producing at its sustainable potential output (\(Y = Y^*\)).






NoteClear It Up: Full Employment Does Not Mean Zero Unemployment



Students often assume that ``full employment’’ means \(u = 0\%\). In macroeconomics, full employment means \(u = u^*\) (zero cyclical unemployment, \(u_c = 0\)), not zero total unemployment. In a dynamic economy where firms continually innovate, new graduates enter the labor force, and workers relocate for better career fits, a positive baseline of frictional and structural unemployment (\(u_f + u_s > 0\)) is always present. Pushing actual unemployment persistently below \(u^*\) creates labor shortages and upward wage-price inflation pressure rather than sustainable output gains.




Visual Representation
Figure 3 illustrates how institutional and behavioral wage rigidities generate structural unemployment in an aggregate labor market. At the market-clearing real wage \((W/P)^*\), labor demand \(L_D\) equals labor supply \(L_S\) at employment \(L^*\). When a binding wage floor—such as a statutory minimum wage, collective bargaining agreement, or efficiency wage—holds the real wage at \((W/P)_{\text{floor}} > (W/P)^*\), firms reduce hiring to \(L_D\) while more workers seek jobs at \(L_S\), creating persistent structural joblessness equal to \(L_S - L_D\).



Figure 3. Wage Rigidity and Structural Unemployment Above the Market-Clearing Real Wage.




Mathematical Foundation
Observed unemployment decomposes additively into its natural and cyclical components: \[\begin{align}
u &= u_f + u_s + u_c \label{eq:u_decomp} \\
u^* &= u_f + u_s \label{eq:natural_rate} \\
u_c &= u - u^* \label{eq:cyclical_u}
\end{align}\] When \(u > u^*\), the labor market exhibits positive cyclical unemployment (\(u_c > 0\)), signaling economic slack. When \(u < u^*\), cyclical unemployment is negative (\(u_c < 0\)), signaling an overheated labor market where employers bid up wages to fill vacancies.


Real-World Application
Three primary institutional and microeconomic mechanisms prevent real wages from falling to clear excess labor supply, thereby shaping the natural rate \(u^*\): [leftmargin=1.5em, itemsep=3pt] * Minimum Wage Laws: Statutory wage floors bind primarily for younger, less-experienced, or entry-level workers whose marginal revenue product lies below the mandated wage. While modest increases often have small employment effects in concentrated local labor markets, steep wage floors above local equilibrium productivity expand \(L_S - L_D\). * Collective Bargaining and Union Contracts: Labor unions negotiate multi-year wage scales and benefit packages above competitive spot-market levels. Insiders who retain positions earn higher compensation, while outsiders queue for scarce union openings. * Efficiency Wages: Even without government mandates or unions, firms voluntarily pay above-market wages to boost worker morale, reduce costly turnover, attract higher-ability applicants, and deter shirking when effort is costly to monitor (as in the Shapiro–Stiglitz shirking model or Akerlof’s gift-exchange framework).
Alongside wage rigidities, the design of Unemployment Insurance (UI) and demographic composition influence \(u^*\). Generous UI replacement rates cushion household consumption during job transitions and allow workers to hold out for better skill matches, but they also lower the opportunity cost of remaining unemployed, slightly lengthening average search spells and raising \(u_f\). Demographics also shift \(u^*\) slowly over decades: younger workers exhibit higher job-separation rates (\(s\)) as they sample careers, so the aging of the U.S. workforce since the 1980s exerted downward secular pressure on \(u^*\), partially offsetting structural skill-mismatch shocks from automation and global trade.

title: 6  Ch06 Unemployment
section: 6.4 The Beveridge Curve and Okun’s Law
text:
6.4 The Beveridge Curve and Okun’s Law

Conceptual Introduction
To diagnose whether rising unemployment stems from a temporary shortfall in aggregate demand or a deeper breakdown in labor-market matching, macroeconomists rely on two empirical pillars: the Beveridge Curve and Okun’s Law.
The Beveridge Curve maps the inverse empirical relationship between the job vacancy rate (\(v\))—measured by the BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) as unfilled job openings divided by employment plus openings—and the unemployment rate (\(u\)). During an economic boom, firms post abundant vacancies while few workers remain unemployed (high \(v\), low \(u\)). During a recession, firms freeze hiring and lay off staff, causing vacancies to collapse as unemployment climbs (low \(v\), high \(u\)). Crucially, business-cycle fluctuations generate movements along a stable Beveridge Curve, whereas changes in matching efficiency—such as geographic immobility, skill obsolescence, or shifts in remote-work preferences—cause the entire curve to shift inward or outward.
Okun’s Law connects the labor market directly to the goods market by quantifying the inverse relationship between cyclical unemployment (\(u - u^*\)) and the percentage output gap \(\left(\frac{Y - Y^*}{Y^*}\right)\), where \(Y\) is actual real GDP and \(Y^*\) is potential real GDP. Because idle workers produce zero output and recessions also reduce average hours worked and capital utilization, every \(1\text{-percentage-point}\) rise in unemployment above \(u^*\) corresponds to a roughly \(2\%\) shortfall in real GDP below potential.


Visual Representation
Figure 4 presents both relationships side by side in standardized graphical form: Panel~(a) contrasts a cyclical movement along the Beveridge Curve (\(A \to B\)) with an outward structural shift (\(A \to C\)), while Panel~(b) depicts the downward-sloping Okun’s Law locus linking labor market slack to the real GDP output gap.



Figure 4. Cyclical Movements vs. Structural Shifts on the Beveridge Curve and Okun’s Law.




Mathematical Foundation
In level-gap form, Okun’s Law states that the percentage deviation of actual real GDP (\(Y\)) from potential real GDP (\(Y^*\)) is proportional to the cyclical unemployment gap (\(u - u^*\)):
\[
\frac{Y - Y^*}{Y^*} = -\beta (u - u^*)
\label{eq:okun_gap}
\]
where \(\beta > 0\) is the Okun coefficient (empirically \(\beta \approx 2.0\) for the United States). Multiplying both sides by \(Y^*\) yields the dollar output shortfall:
\[
Y - Y^* = -\beta (u - u^*) Y^*
\label{eq:okun_dollar}
\]
Notice why \(\beta > 1\): a \(1\%\) decline in employment does not merely lower output by \(1\%\); it is accompanied by reduced overtime hours, lower labor force participation, and underutilized factory capacity, amplifying the total GDP loss to roughly \(2\%\).
Flagship Baseline Calculation. Suppose potential output is \(Y^* = \$25.0\text{ trillion}\), the natural rate of unemployment is \(u^* = 4.50\%\), the actual unemployment rate is \(u = 6.50\%\), and the Okun coefficient is \(\beta = 2.0\). Substituting into Equations~\(\eqref{eq:okun_gap}\) and~\(\eqref{eq:okun_dollar}\):
\[
\frac{Y - Y^*}{Y^*} = -2.0 \times (0.065 - 0.045) = -2.0 \times 0.020 = -0.040 = -4.00\%
\]
\[
Y - Y^* = -0.040 \times \$25.0\text{ trillion} = -\$1.0\text{ trillion}
\]
Actual real GDP equals \(Y = \$24.0\text{ trillion}\), representing a cyclical output shortfall of \(\$1.0\text{ trillion}\).


Real-World Application
Historically, Okun’s Law has also reliably tracked major U.S. business cycles. During the 1982 recession, unemployment peaked at \(10.8\%\) against an estimated natural rate near \(6.0\%\) (\(u - u^* \approx +4.8\%\)), coinciding with a severe real GDP gap approaching \(-9\%\). Similarly, during the Great Recession of 2009, unemployment reached \(10.0\%\) against \(u^* \approx 4.8\%\), implying an output gap of roughly \(-10\%\) and trillions of dollars in forgone national income.

Chapter Summary and Practice

Check Your Understanding
[leftmargin=1.5em, itemsep=6pt] * BLS Classification and Rates: An economy has a Civilian Noninstitutional Population of \(P = 250.0\text{ million}\), of whom \(142.5\text{ million}\) are employed and \(7.5\text{ million}\) are unemployed. Among those not in the labor force, \(4.0\text{ million}\) are marginally attached (including \(1.5\text{ million}\) discouraged workers), while \(6.0\text{ million}\) of the employed are working part-time for economic reasons. Compute: (a) the Labor Force (\(\text{LF}\)), (b) \(\text{LFPR}\), (c) \(\text{EPOP}\), (d) headline \(\text{U-3}\), and (e) broad \(\text{U-6}\). * Labor Force Exit Dynamics: Starting from the baseline economy in Question~1, suppose \(1.5\text{ million}\) unemployed workers become discouraged and stop searching for jobs, while employment remains unchanged at \(142.5\text{ million}\). Calculate the new \(\text{U-3}\) rate and explain why the direction of change can mislead casual observers. * Wage Floors and Steady-State Flows: (a) Using a labor supply and demand framework, explain how an increase in a binding minimum wage affects employment, labor force participation, and structural unemployment. (b) In a dynamic labor market with a monthly separation rate of \(s = 1.2\%\) and a monthly job-finding rate of \(f = 22.8\%\), compute the steady-state natural rate of unemployment \(u^*\). * Beveridge Curve and Okun’s Law: Suppose an economy has potential real GDP \(Y^* = \$28.0\text{ trillion}\), a natural rate of unemployment \(u^* = 4.2\%\), an actual unemployment rate \(u = 5.7\%\), and an Okun coefficient \(\beta = 2.0\). (a) Calculate the percentage output gap and the dollar shortfall \(Y - Y^*\). (b) If job vacancies simultaneously fell sharply while unemployment rose from \(4.2\%\) to \(5.7\%\), did the economy experience a movement along the Beveridge Curve or an outward shift? Explain. * Growth-Rate Okun’s Law: Suppose trend potential GDP growth in an economy is \(g_{Y^*} = 2.4\%\) per year and the Okun coefficient is \(\beta = 2.0\). (a) If actual real GDP grows by \(1.4\%\) over the year, by how many percentage points does the unemployment rate change (\(\Delta u\))? (b) What real GDP growth rate is required to reduce the unemployment rate by \(0.75\text{ percentage points}\) over a single year? * CPS vs. CES Divergence: During the early stages of an economic recovery, analysts observe that nonfarm payroll employment (CES) increases by \(250{,}000\) jobs while the household survey unemployment rate (U-3) simultaneously rises from \(5.2\%\) to \(5.4\%\). Explain how both statistics can be accurate at the same time.


Worked Solutions
[leftmargin=1.5em, itemsep=6pt] * BLS Classification and Rates: [leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=2pt] (a) \(\text{LF} = E + U = 142.5 + 7.5 = 150.0\text{ million}\). (b) \(\text{LFPR} = \frac{\text{LF}}{P} \times 100 = \frac{150.0}{250.0} \times 100 = 60.00\%\). (c) \(\text{EPOP} = \frac{E}{P} \times 100 = \frac{142.5}{250.0} \times 100 = 57.00\%\). (d) \(\text{U-3} = \frac{U}{\text{LF}} \times 100 = \frac{7.5}{150.0} \times 100 = 5.00\%\). (e) Note that discouraged workers (\(1.5\text{M}\)) are already counted inside \(M = 4.0\text{M}\), so they are not added separately:
\[
\text{U-6} = \frac{U + M + PT_{\text{econ}}}{\text{LF} + M} \times 100 = \frac{7.5 + 4.0 + 6.0}{150.0 + 4.0} \times 100 = \frac{17.5}{154.0} \times 100 \approx 11.36\%.
\]

Labor Force Exit Dynamics: When \(1.5\text{ million}\) unemployed workers stop searching, they leave both \(U\) and \(\text{LF}\):

\[
U_{\text{new}} = 7.5 - 1.5 = 6.0\text{ million}, \qquad \text{LF}_{\text{new}} = 142.5 + 6.0 = 148.5\text{ million}
\]
\[
\text{U-3}_{\text{new}} = \frac{6.0}{148.5} \times 100 \approx 4.04\%
\]
Headline \(\text{U-3}\) falls by \(0.96\text{ percentage points}\) (from \(5.00\%\) to \(4.04\%\)) even though zero jobs were created, because the numerator fell proportionally faster than the denominator. Meanwhile, \(\text{U-6}\) remains unchanged at \(11.36\%\) because those \(1.5\text{ million}\) workers simply shifted from \(U\) to \(M\).

Wage Floors and Steady-State Flows: [leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=2pt]


Raising a binding wage floor further above \((W/P)^*\) moves firms up along the downward-sloping labor demand curve \(L_D\) (reducing employment) and attracts additional job seekers up along the upward-sloping labor supply curve \(L_S\) (increasing labor force participation). Both effects widen the structural surplus \(L_S - L_D\).
Using the Markov steady-state flow equation with \(s = 0.012\) and \(f = 0.228\):

\[
u^* = \frac{s}{s + f} = \frac{0.012}{0.012 + 0.228} = \frac{0.012}{0.240} = 0.050 = 5.00\%.
\]

Beveridge Curve and Okun’s Law: [leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=2pt]


Cyclical unemployment is \(u - u^* = 5.7\% - 4.2\% = +1.5\%\). Applying Okun’s Law:

\[
\frac{Y - Y^*}{Y^*} = -2.0 \times 0.015 = -0.030 = -3.00\%
\]
\[
Y - Y^* = -0.030 \times \$28.0\text{ trillion} = -\$0.84\text{ trillion}\;(-\$840\text{ billion}).
\]

A simultaneous drop in job vacancies and rise in unemployment represents a downward-right movement along the existing Beveridge Curve, driven by a negative aggregate demand shock rather than a structural deterioration in matching efficiency.


Growth-Rate Okun’s Law: [leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=2pt]


Using \(g_Y - g_{Y^*} = -\beta \Delta u\) with \(g_Y = 1.4\%\), \(g_{Y^*} = 2.4\%\), and \(\beta = 2.0\):

\[
1.4\% - 2.4\% = -2.0 \Delta u \implies -1.0\% = -2.0 \Delta u \implies \Delta u = +0.50\text{ percentage points}.
\]
Because output grew more slowly than potential trend growth, unemployment rises by \(0.50\text{ percentage points}\). (b) Setting \(\Delta u = -0.75\%\):
\[
g_Y = g_{Y^*} - \beta \Delta u = 2.4\% - 2.0(-0.75\%) = 2.4\% + 1.5\% = 3.90\%.
\]

CPS vs. CES Divergence: First, an improving job market frequently draws previously discouraged or marginally attached workers back into active job search (\(\text{NILF} \to U\)). Because these re-entrants are counted in \(U\) before securing an offer, \(\text{U-3} = U / (E + U)\) can temporarily tick upward even as hiring expands. Second, if existing workers take on second jobs, CES establishment payrolls record each new position while CPS household employment counts each individual only once.
