title: 7  Chapter 7: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
section: 7.1 Saving Flows, Wealth Stocks, and Macroeconomic Investment
text:
7.1 Saving Flows, Wealth Stocks, and Macroeconomic Investment

Conceptual Introduction
 In everyday conversation, people use saving'' andwealth’’ interchangeably, yet macroeconomics draws a strict boundary between a flow and a stock. Saving (\(S\)) is a flow variable: it measures the portion of current disposable income (\(Y_d\)) that a household, business, or government chooses not to spend on current consumption during a specific time interval, such as a month, quarter, or year. By contrast, wealth (\(W\)) is a stock variable: it measures the total net value of assets (bank deposits, bonds, equities, real estate, minus debts) owned at a single point in time. Positive saving acts like water flowing into a bathtub—each month of positive saving raises the water level of accumulated wealth, whereas negative saving (dissaving, when spending exceeds current income) drains the stock of wealth.
Understanding how wealth evolves also requires separating active saving flows from asset valuation changes. A household’s net worth can rise over a year either because the household actively refrains from consuming part of its paycheck (\(S > 0\)) or because the market price of existing assets it already owns—such as a home or stock index fund—appreciates (capital gains). Conversely, falling asset prices (capital losses) can reduce household wealth even when a family continues to save out of every paycheck. Tracking both the saving flow and balance-sheet asset valuations explains why household spending responds sharply to housing and stock market swings.
Equally critical is the macroeconomic distinction between physical investment (\(I\)) and financial investment. In macroeconomic accounting (NIPA), investment refers exclusively to spending on newly produced physical capital goods—such as factory machinery, commercial buildings, software, cloud servers, and additions to business inventories—that expand the economy’s future productive capacity. When an individual buys shares of an existing corporation on the New York Stock Exchange or purchases an existing suburban house, no new physical capital is created; ownership of an existing asset simply transfers from seller to buyer. In macroeconomics, buying stocks or bonds is household saving (supplying funds to the financial system), whereas a firm using borrowed funds to build a new warehouse is investment.


Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates the stock–flow relationship over a five-year horizon for a household starting with zero initial wealth (\(W_0 = \$0\)). Each vertical bar represents the annual saving flow (\(S_t\)), while the connected trajectory tracks cumulative end-of-year wealth (\(W_t = \sum_{k=1}^{t} S_k\)). Notice that even when the annual saving flow dips in Years 3 and 4, cumulative wealth continues rising because every positive flow adds to the existing stock.



Figure 1. Annual Saving (Flow) vs. Cumulative Wealth (Stock). Blue bars measure annual saving flows (\(S_t\): \(\$5\text{k}, \$10\text{k}, \$8\text{k}, \$7\text{k}, \$9\text{k}\)), whereas the orange trajectory tracks the accumulated stock of wealth (\(W_t\): \(\$5\text{k}, \$15\text{k}, \$23\text{k}, \$30\text{k}, \$39\text{k}\)).




Real-World Application: U.S. Household Saving Rate Swings
The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis tracks household saving flows relative to disposable personal income through the Personal Saving Rate (FRED: ). During the 2007–2009 Great Recession, collapsing home prices and equity values erased trillions of dollars in household wealth; in response, families cut discretionary consumption and raised their personal saving rate from roughly \(2.5\%\) in 2007 to over \(6\%\) by 2009 to rebuild depleted wealth buffers. A decade later, during the 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns, pandemic stimulus transfers combined with closed restaurants and travel restrictions pushed above \(30\%\) in April 2020, creating a massive stock of ``excess savings’’ that fueled consumer spending through 2022–2023 before the saving rate normalized near \(4\%\)–\(5\%\) in 2024–2026.






NoteClear It Up: Economic Investment vs. Financial Investment



Students frequently lose points on exams by labeling stock or bond purchases as ``investment.’’ In macroeconomics: [noitemsep] * Financial Investment (Household Saving): Buying stocks, corporate bonds, Treasury bills, or existing real estate transfers ownership of existing claims and supplies funds to financial markets. * Physical Investment (\(I\) in GDP): Firms purchasing newly manufactured machinery, commercial structures, software, or residential construction adds directly to the nation’s capital stock (\(K\)).




Mathematical Foundation
Let disposable income in period \(t\) be \(Y_{d,t} = Y_t + TR_t - T_t\) (total income plus government transfers minus taxes) and household consumption spending be \(C_t\). Household saving flow in period \(t\) is:
\[
S_t = Y_{d,t} - C_t
\]
Given beginning-of-period wealth \(W_{t-1}\) and net capital gains \(\Delta V_t\) on existing assets, end-of-period wealth evolves according to the stock–flow accumulation identity:
\[
W_t = W_{t-1} + S_t + \Delta V_t
\]






TipWork It Out: Calculating Saving Flows and Ending Wealth



Suppose a household begins the year with \(W_0 = \$120{,}000\) in financial and housing assets. During the year, the household earns \(\$95{,}000\) in gross income, pays \(\$15{,}000\) in taxes, receives \(\$0\) in transfers, and spends \(\$68{,}000\) on consumption goods and services. Meanwhile, its existing retirement index fund rises in market value by \(\Delta V_1 = +\$6{,}000\).

Compute Disposable Income (\(Y_{d,1}\)): \[Y_{d,1} = \$95{,}000 + \$0 - \$15{,}000 = \$80{,}000\]
Compute Annual Saving Flow (\(S_1\)): \[S_1 = Y_{d,1} - C_1 = \$80{,}000 - \$68{,}000 = \$12{,}000\] The household’s personal saving rate is \(\frac{\$12{,}000}{\$80{,}000} \times 100 = 15.0\%\).
Compute End-of-Year Wealth Stock (\(W_1\)): \[W_1 = W_0 + S_1 + \Delta V_1 = \$120{,}000 + \$12{,}000 + \$6{,}000 = \$138{,}000\]









Note[Advanced: For Economics Majors] Continuous-Time Wealth Accumulation



In continuous time, let \(w(t)\) denote the real wealth stock at instant \(t\), \(s(t) = y_d(t) - c(t)\) denote the instantaneous saving flow rate, and \(r_a\) denote the real capital-gain rate on existing assets. Wealth evolves according to the first-order linear differential equation: \[\frac{dw(t)}{dt} = s(t) + r_a w(t)\] Integrating from \(t = 0\) to \(T\) yields \(w(T) = w(0)e^{r_a T} + \int_0^T s(\tau)e^{r_a(T-\tau)}\,d\tau\), showing how early saving flows compound across time.

text:
7.2 National Saving and the Open-Economy Identity

Conceptual Introduction
To understand how an entire nation finances physical capital investment, we scale up from an individual household to the macroeconomy using the National Income and Product Accounts (NIPA) expenditure identity: \(Y = C + I + G + NX\). In any economy, total output produced (\(Y\)) that is neither consumed by households (\(C\)) nor purchased by government agencies (\(G\)) represents output set aside from current consumption—which is the macroeconomic definition of national saving (\(S\)).
National saving is generated by two domestic sectors. Private saving (\(S_p\)) is the disposable income households and firms retain after paying net taxes (\(T_{\text{net}} = T - TR\)) and purchasing consumption goods: \(S_p = Y - T_{\text{net}} - C\). Public saving (\(S_g\)) is the difference between government net tax revenue and government purchases of goods and services: \(S_g = T_{\text{net}} - G\). When \(T_{\text{net}} > G\), the government runs a budget surplus (\(S_g > 0\)) and adds to national saving; when \(T_{\text{net}} < G\), the government runs a budget deficit (\(S_g < 0\)), reducing national saving.
Linking national saving to domestic investment depends on whether the economy interacts financially with the rest of the world. In a closed economy (\(NX = 0\)), every dollar of domestic investment must be financed by domestic saving, yielding the closed-economy saving–investment identity \(S = I\). In an open economy, domestic investment can exceed domestic national saving (\(I > S\)) if foreign savers lend funds to domestic borrowers. Because a trade deficit (\(NX < 0\), meaning imports exceed exports) leaves foreign trading partners holding domestic currency that they reinvest in domestic bonds, stocks, and factories, net capital inflow (\(NCI\)) equals the negative of net exports (\(NCI = -NX\)), giving the open-economy funding identity \(I = S_p + S_g + NCI\).


Visual Representation
Figure 2 compares how domestic physical investment (\(I\)) is financed under closed-economy versus open-economy accounting. In the left panel (Closed Economy), domestic investment equals national saving (\(I = S_p + S_g\)). In the right panel (Open Economy with a budget deficit \(S_g < 0\) and a trade deficit \(NX < 0\)), positive net capital inflows (\(NCI = -NX > 0\)) supplement private saving to fund total domestic investment.



Figure 2. Closed vs. Open Economy Saving–Investment Accounting. In a closed economy (Panel A), national saving (\(S_p + S_g\)) exactly equals domestic investment (\(I\)). In an open economy running both a budget deficit (\(S_g < 0\)) and a trade deficit (\(NX < 0\)), net capital inflows (\(NCI = -NX > 0\)) help finance domestic investment and public borrowing (Panel B).




Real-World Application: U.S. Twin Deficits and Foreign Capital Inflows
In recent U.S. macroeconomic data, Gross Private Domestic Investment (FRED: ) has consistently exceeded domestic national saving because Net Government Saving (FRED: ) has been deeply negative while private saving remains moderate. How does the United States sustain high domestic capital formation despite low net national saving? Foreign central banks, sovereign wealth funds, and international private investors purchase U.S. Treasury securities, corporate bonds, and equities—generating positive Net Capital Inflows (\(NCI > 0\)) that mirror the U.S. current account (trade) deficit (\(NX < 0\)).






NoteClear It Up: Accounting Identities Do Not Prove Causation



The open-economy identity \(S - I = NX\) (or \(I = S + NCI\)) holds ex post by national accounting definition, just as \(2 + 2 = 4\) is always true. However, an accounting identity alone does not tell us whether a fall in national saving caused a trade deficit or whether strong foreign demand for U.S. assets drove capital inflows (\(NCI > 0\)) that appreciated the dollar and widened the trade deficit (\(NX < 0\)). Economists use behavioral models (such as the loanable-funds market) to establish causal mechanisms.




Mathematical Foundation
Starting from the aggregate expenditure identity \(Y = C + I + G + NX\), subtract \(C\) and \(G\) from both sides:
\[
Y - C - G = I + NX
\]
Add and subtract net taxes \(T_{\text{net}} = T - TR\) on the left-hand side to separate private saving (\(S_p\)) and public saving (\(S_g\)):
\[
S = \underbrace{(Y - T_{\text{net}} - C)}_{S_p} + \underbrace{(T_{\text{net}} - G)}_{S_g} = Y - C - G
\]
Substituting \(S = Y - C - G\) and defining Net Capital Inflow as \(NCI = -NX\) (capital inflows from abroad minus capital outflows to abroad) yields the closed- and open-economy investment identities:
\[
\text{Closed Economy } (NX = 0): \quad I = S = S_p + S_g
\]
\[
\text{Open Economy } (NCI = -NX): \quad I = S + NCI = S_p + S_g + NCI
\]






TipWork It Out: Decomposing National Saving and Net Capital Inflows



Suppose an open economy has GDP of \(Y = \$20{,}000\text{ billion}\), household consumption \(C = \$13{,}600\text{ billion}\), government purchases \(G = \$3{,}400\text{ billion}\), net tax collections \(T_{\text{net}} = \$3{,}000\text{ billion}\), and domestic physical investment \(I = \$3{,}600\text{ billion}\).

Calculate Private Saving (\(S_p\)): \[S_p = Y - T_{\text{net}} - C = \$20{,}000 - \$3{,}000 - \$13{,}600 = \$3{,}400\text{ billion}\]
Calculate Public Saving (\(S_g\)): \[S_g = T_{\text{net}} - G = \$3{,}000 - \$3{,}400 = -\$400\text{ billion} \quad (\text{a } \$400\text{B budget deficit})\]
Calculate National Saving (\(S\)): \[S = S_p + S_g = \$3{,}400 + (-\$400) = \$3{,}000\text{ billion}\]
Calculate Net Capital Inflow (\(NCI\)) and Net Exports (\(NX\)): \[NCI = I - S = \$3{,}600 - \$3{,}000 = +\$600\text{ billion}\] \[NX = -NCI = -\$600\text{ billion} \quad (\text{a } \$600\text{B trade deficit financed by foreign saving})\]

section: 7.3 The Financial System: Assets, Intermediaries, and Core Tasks
text:
7.3 The Financial System: Assets, Intermediaries, and Core Tasks

Conceptual Introduction
National saving cannot automatically transform into factories, power grids, and software unless an institutional mechanism connects millions of small household savers with businesses seeking large sums for long-term capital projects. The financial system consists of the markets and institutions that channel funds from savers (lenders) to investors (borrowers). Savers supply funds by acquiring financial assets—paper or electronic claims that entitle the buyer to future income from the seller—including loans (direct debt contracts), bonds (tradeable IOUs promising fixed interest payments and principal repayment at maturity), stocks (shares of partial ownership in a corporation), and bank deposits.
Rather than requiring every household to vet individual corporate borrowers directly, modern economies rely heavily on financial intermediaries—institutions that transform funds gathered from many individuals into financial assets. Major intermediaries include commercial banks (which accept liquid checking and savings deposits and originate business and mortgage loans), mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) (which pool saver money to buy diversified portfolios of stocks and bonds), pension funds (which invest worker retirement contributions over multi-decade horizons), and life insurance companies.
Across all these institutions, a well-functioning financial system performs three indispensable macroeconomic tasks: [noitemsep] * Reducing Transaction Costs: Standardized bond markets and bank lending departments eliminate the prohibitive search, legal, and credit-monitoring costs that would arise if an individual saver tried to negotiate loans directly with thousands of firms. * Reducing Risk through Diversification: Because future business profits are uncertain, investing all of one’s savings in a single company exposes a household to idiosyncratic failure. Mutual funds and banks pool funds across hundreds of firms and industries, allowing savers to earn steady average returns while shedding firm-specific risk. * Providing Liquidity: Businesses need funds locked into machinery for years, whereas households want rapid access to cash for emergencies. Banks and secondary stock/bond markets provide liquidity—the ability to convert an asset into spendable cash quickly without significant loss of value.


Visual Representation
Figure 3 maps the architecture of the financial system, showing how household and foreign saving flows through both direct financial markets (stocks and bonds) and financial intermediaries (banks, mutual funds, pension funds) to finance business capital formation while performing the three core financial tasks.



Figure 3. Architecture of the Financial System. Funds flow from domestic and foreign savers either directly through bond and stock markets or indirectly through financial intermediaries to finance physical investment (\(I\)).




Real-World Application: Index Funds and Liquidity Mismatch Risks
Consider how retail index mutual funds and ETFs democratized diversification: for an expense ratio below \(0.05\%\) per year, a first-time investor with \(\$500\) can own fractional shares of 500 major U.S. corporations, achieving near-complete diversification of idiosyncratic firm risk at minimal transaction cost. Conversely, when financial intermediaries mismanage liquidity transformation, systemic fragility emerges. In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) held long-term fixed-rate Treasury bonds funded by uninsured, instantly withdrawable tech-startup deposits. When rising interest rates lowered the market value of SVB’s long-term bonds and depositors triggered rapid digital withdrawals, SVB suffered an acute liquidity run—illustrating why bank capital and liquidity regulations are essential to financial stability.


Mathematical Foundation
Two foundational quantitative relationships govern financial assets:

Inverse Relationship Between Bond Prices and Interest Rates: For a one-year zero-coupon bond paying face value \(F\) at maturity and selling today at market price \(P_B\), the nominal yield (interest rate) \(i\) is:

\[
i = \frac{F - P_B}{P_B} \iff P_B = \frac{F}{1 + i}
\]
When market interest rates \(i\) rise, the market price \(P_B\) of existing fixed-payment bonds must fall so new buyers earn the competitive market yield. * The Fisher Equation (Real vs. Nominal Interest Rates): Because inflation erodes the purchasing power of repaid dollars, borrowers and lenders evaluate the real interest rate (\(r\)), approximated by subtracting expected inflation (\(\pi^e\)) from the nominal interest rate (\(i\)):
\[
r \approx i - \pi^e \qquad \left(\text{exact formula: } 1 + r = \frac{1 + i}{1 + \pi^e}\right)
\]






TipWork It Out: Bond Pricing, Real Yields, and Risk Diversification




Bond Price and Yield: A one-year U.S. Treasury bill has a face value of \(F = \$1{,}000\) and trades today at \(P_B = \$950\). Its nominal interest rate is: \[i = \frac{\$1{,}000 - \$950}{\$950} = \frac{\$50}{\$950} \approx 0.0526 \quad (5.26\%)\] If market interest rates rise to \(i' = 6.0\%\), the bond’s market price drops to: \[P_B' = \frac{\$1{,}000}{1.06} \approx \$943.40\]
Real Interest Rate: If the nominal bond yield is \(i = 5.26\%\) and expected inflation is \(\pi^e = 2.26\%\), the expected real return to the saver is: \[r \approx 5.26\% - 2.26\% = 3.00\%\]
Diversification Math: Suppose each independent biotech startup has an annual return standard deviation of \(\sigma = 40\%\). An equally weighted mutual fund holding \(N = 100\) uncorrelated startups reduces portfolio volatility to: \[\sigma_p = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{N}} = \frac{40\%}{\sqrt{100}} = \frac{40\%}{10} = 4.0\%\]









Note[Advanced: For Economics Majors] Multi-Year Bond Valuation and Duration



For a multi-year bond paying annual coupon \(C\) for \(T\) years plus face value \(F\) at maturity, its present discounted value at yield \(i\) is: \[P_B(i) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{C}{(1+i)^t} + \frac{F}{(1+i)^T}\] Differentiating with respect to \(i\) yields \(\frac{dP_B}{di} = -\frac{D_{\text{Mac}}}{1+i} P_B < 0\), where \(D_{\text{Mac}}\) is Macaulay duration. Longer-maturity bonds have higher duration and suffer larger percentage price drops when interest rates rise.

section: 7.4 The Market for Loanable Funds
text:
7.4 The Market for Loanable Funds

Conceptual Introduction
Economists model how the financial system coordinates saving and investment using the market for loanable funds—a hypothetical market that brings together all savers who want to lend funds and all borrowers who want to finance investment spending. The ``price’’ in this market is the real interest rate (\(r\)), which measures the inflation-adjusted return earned by lenders and the inflation-adjusted cost paid by borrowers.
The demand for loanable funds (\(I\)) comes from firms (and homebuyers) borrowing to finance physical investment projects, and it slopes downward. A firm undertakes a capital project only if its expected rate of return meets or exceeds the real interest rate (\(r\)). When \(r\) is high (say, \(7\%\)), only highly profitable projects pass this hurdle, so the quantity of loanable funds demanded is low. When \(r\) falls (say, to \(3\%\)), many additional warehouse, factory, and equipment projects become profitable, increasing the quantity of investment funds demanded. Any change in perceived business opportunities—such as a breakthrough in artificial intelligence or an investment tax credit—shifts the entire investment demand curve rightward.
The supply of loanable funds (\(S\)) comes from national saving (private plus public saving) and net capital inflows, and it slopes upward. Households face an intertemporal trade-off between consuming today versus consuming in the future; a higher real interest rate raises the reward for deferring consumption, inducing households to save more and attracting foreign capital inflows. Changes in household thrift, tax incentives for retirement accounts (such as 401(k) or Roth IRA expansions), foreign capital flows, or government budget balances shift the supply curve of loanable funds. At the equilibrium real interest rate \(r^*\), the quantity of loanable funds supplied exactly equals the quantity demanded (\(Q_S(r^*) = Q_D(r^*) = Q^*\)).


Visual Representation
Figure 4 depicts equilibrium in the market for loanable funds. The downward-sloping investment demand curve (\(I\): \(r = 8.0 - 0.03Q\)) intersects the upward-sloping supply curve (\(S\): \(r = 1.0 + 0.02Q\)) at point \(E^*\), establishing an equilibrium real interest rate of \(r^* = 3.8\%\) and equilibrium loanable funds of \(Q^* = \$140\text{ billion}\). At any rate above equilibrium (such as \(r = 5.0\%\)), desired saving (\(\$200\text{B}\)) exceeds desired investment (\(\$100\text{B}\)), creating a \(\$100\text{B}\) surplus of funds that drives \(r\) down toward \(3.8\%\).



Figure 4. Loanable Funds Market Equilibrium. Upward-sloping supply \(S\) (\(r = 1.0 + 0.02Q\)) intersects downward-sloping investment demand \(I\) (\(r = 8.0 - 0.03Q\)) at \(Q^* = \$140\text{ billion}\) and \(r^* = 3.8\%\).




Real-World Application: Real Treasury Yields and Corporate Investment Hurdles
Financial analysts monitor the 10-Year Treasury Inflation-Indexed Security yield (FRED: ) alongside the nominal 10-Year Treasury yield (FRED: ) as a real-time barometer of the economy’s benchmark real interest rate. Between 2020 and 2021, hovered near \(-1.0\%\), encouraging aggressive corporate borrowing for warehouse expansion, residential construction, and software investment. By 2024–2026, as rose near \(+1.8\%\) to \(+2.1\%\), capital-intensive housing and commercial real estate projects faced much steeper borrowing hurdles, shifting private investment toward high-expected-return sectors such as artificial intelligence infrastructure and semiconductor manufacturing.


Mathematical Foundation
Let the supply of loanable funds (\(Q_S\), in billions of dollars) and the investment demand for loanable funds (\(Q_D\), in billions of dollars) be linear functions of the real interest rate \(r\) (measured in percentage points): \[\begin{align}
\text{Supply of Loanable Funds:} \quad & Q_S = -50 + 50r \qquad \left(\text{inverse: } r = 1.0 + 0.02Q_S\right) \\
\text{Investment Demand:} \quad & Q_D = \frac{800 - 100r}{3} \qquad \left(\text{inverse: } r = 8.0 - 0.03Q_D\right)
\end{align}\] Market equilibrium requires \(Q_S(r^*) = Q_D(r^*)\), or equivalently equating the inverse supply and demand curves at \(Q^*\).






TipWork It Out: Solving for Loanable-Funds Equilibrium and Disequilibrium



Using the supply curve \(r = 1.0 + 0.02Q\) and investment demand curve \(r = 8.0 - 0.03Q\) plotted in Figure 4:

Find Equilibrium Quantity (\(Q^*\)): Set inverse supply equal to inverse demand: \[1.0 + 0.02Q^* = 8.0 - 0.03Q^*\] \[0.05Q^* = 7.0 \implies Q^* = \frac{7.0}{0.05} = \$140\text{ billion}\]
Find Equilibrium Real Interest Rate (\(r^*\)): Substitute \(Q^* = 140\) into either curve: \[r^* = 1.0 + 0.02(140) = 1.0 + 2.8 = 3.8\%\]
Verify Disequilibrium at \(r = 5.0\%\): [noitemsep]
Quantity supplied: \(Q_S = -50 + 50(5.0) = \$200\text{ billion}\).
Quantity demanded: \(Q_D = \frac{800 - 100(5.0)}{3} = \frac{300}{3} = \$100\text{ billion}\).
Excess supply (surplus) \(= \$200\text{B} - \$100\text{B} = \$100\text{ billion}\), putting downward pressure on \(r\) until \(r^* = 3.8\%\).









Note[Advanced: For Economics Majors] Two-Period Intertemporal Optimization



A representative household maximizes lifetime utility \(U(C_1, C_2) = u(C_1) + \beta u(C_2)\) subject to the intertemporal budget constraint \(C_1 + \frac{C_2}{1+r} = Y_1 + \frac{Y_2}{1+r}\), where \(\beta \in (0,1)\) is the subjective discount factor. Setting up the Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L} = u(C_1) + \beta u(C_2) + \lambda\left(Y_1 - C_1 + \frac{Y_2 - C_2}{1+r}\right)\) yields the consumption Euler equation: \[\frac{u'(C_1)}{\beta u'(C_2)} = 1 + r\] When \(r\) rises, the relative price of current consumption (\(1+r\)) increases, inducing the household to substitute away from \(C_1\) and increase saving \(S_1 = Y_1 - C_1\) (assuming the substitution effect dominates the income effect).

section: 7.5 Government Budget Deficits, Interest Rates, and Crowding Out
text:
7.5 Government Budget Deficits, Interest Rates, and Crowding Out

Conceptual Introduction
Because national saving equals the sum of private saving and public saving (\(S = S_p + S_g\)), fiscal policy directly affects the supply of loanable funds. When the federal government increases spending (\(G\)) or cuts taxes (\(T\)) without offsetting revenue, its budget balance (\(S_g = T_{\text{net}} - G\)) moves into deficit (\(S_g < 0\)). Because the U.S. Treasury must issue government bonds to finance that deficit, it absorbs a share of private saving, shifting the supply of loanable funds leftward at every real interest rate.
The leftward shift in loanable-funds supply creates a temporary shortage of funds at the initial real interest rate \(r_1^*\), bidding the equilibrium real interest rate up to a higher level \(r_2^* > r_1^*\). As borrowing becomes more expensive, private businesses cancel or scale back marginal investment projects, reducing private investment from \(I_1^*\) to \(I_2^*\). Economists call this negative side effect of government budget deficits crowding out: government borrowing drives up real interest rates and reduces private physical investment spending.
Crucially, however, crowding out is typically partial rather than one-for-one. A \(\$50\text{ billion}\) increase in the government budget deficit rarely reduces private investment by the full \(\$50\text{ billion}\) for three reasons: (1) the higher real interest rate \(r_2^*\) induces domestic households to save more along the upward-sloping supply curve, (2) higher U.S. real interest rates attract foreign capital inflows (\(NCI\)) from global savers, and (3) during a deep recession with idle factories and slack labor, increased government spending raises national income (\(Y\)), generating additional private saving and prompting the Federal Reserve to keep policy rates accommodative.


Visual Representation
Figure 5 illustrates a \(\$50\text{ billion}\) budget deficit shock using our baseline curves from Section~7.4. Initially, \(S_0\) (\(r = 1.0 + 0.02Q\)) and \(I\) (\(r = 8.0 - 0.03Q\)) intersect at \(E_1(Q_1^* = \$140\text{B}, r_1^* = 3.8\%)\). A \(\$50\text{ billion}\) deficit shifts supply leftward by \(\$50\text{B}\) at every interest rate to \(S_1\) (\(r = 2.0 + 0.02Q\)). Equilibrium moves to \(E_2(Q_2^* = \$120\text{B}, r_2^* = 4.4\%)\): private investment falls by \(\$20\text{B}\) (partial crowding out), while higher interest rates induce \(+\$30\text{B}\) of additional private saving (from \(\$140\text{B}\) to \(\$170\text{B}\) along \(S_0\)) to absorb the remainder of the \(\$50\text{B}\) deficit. Figure 6 contrasts complete crowding out (vertical supply), partial crowding out (upward-sloping supply), and recessionary/accommodative conditions (flat supply).



Figure 5. Crowding Out in the Loanable Funds Market. A \(\$50\text{ billion}\) budget deficit shifts national saving left from \(S_0\) to \(S_1\), raising \(r^*\) from \(3.8\%\) to \(4.4\%\) and reducing private investment by \(\$20\text{ billion}\) (from \(\$140\text{B}\) to \(\$120\text{B}\)).





Figure 6. Three Regimes of Crowding-Out Magnitude. The sensitivity of saving supply to the real interest rate—and the presence of foreign capital inflows or central bank accommodation—governs how strongly budget deficits crowd out private investment.




Real-World Application: U.S. Federal Deficits and Empirical Crowding Out
Empirical data from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis allow economists to track fiscal deficits alongside real borrowing costs and private investment. Specifically, FRED series measures the annual federal surplus or deficit, reports net government saving across federal, state, and local governments, tracks gross private domestic investment, and measures the 10-year TIPS real interest rate. During the 2009 Great Recession, federal deficits surged above \(\$1.4\text{ trillion}\) while fell below \(1\%\), demonstrating Panel (c) of Figure 6: economic slack and Federal Reserve accommodation prevented interest rate spikes. Conversely, during the full-employment expansion of 2023–2026, persistent structural deficits coincided with rising above \(2\%\), illustrating classic partial crowding out under full capacity.






NoteClear It Up: Why Foreign Capital Inflows Cushion Crowding Out



In an open economy like the United States, a higher real interest rate \(r_2^*\) does not just coax extra saving out of domestic households—it also attracts foreign investors seeking higher real returns on U.S. Treasury bonds. Those foreign capital inflows (\(NCI > 0\)) partially replenish the domestic pool of loanable funds, moderating the rise in \(r^*\) and reducing domestic investment crowding out, though at the cost of a wider trade deficit (\(NX < 0\)) and higher future interest payments to foreign bondholders.




Mathematical Foundation
Let initial loanable-funds supply be \(Q_{S,0} = -50 + 50r\) (where \(S_g = 0\) initially) and investment demand be \(Q_D = \frac{800 - 100r}{3}\). When the government runs a budget deficit of \(\Delta D = \$50\text{ billion}\) (\(S_g' = -\$50\text{B}\)), total national saving shifts leftward by \(\$50\text{B}\) at every interest rate:
\[
Q_{S,1} = Q_{S,0} - \Delta D = (-50 + 50r) - 50 = -100 + 50r \qquad \left(\text{inverse: } r = 2.0 + 0.02Q_{S,1}\right)
\]






TipWork It Out: Quantifying Partial Crowding Out from a $50 Billion Deficit



Using the baseline equilibrium \(E_1(Q_1^* = \$140\text{B}, r_1^* = 3.8\%)\) from Figure 5, trace the impact of a \(\$50\text{ billion}\) government budget deficit:

Solve for Post-Deficit Equilibrium Investment (\(I_2^*\)): Equate the shifted inverse supply \(r = 2.0 + 0.02Q\) to inverse investment demand \(r = 8.0 - 0.03Q\): \[2.0 + 0.02Q_2^* = 8.0 - 0.03Q_2^*\] \[0.05Q_2^* = 6.0 \implies Q_2^* = I_2^* = \frac{6.0}{0.05} = \$120\text{ billion}\]
Solve for Post-Deficit Real Interest Rate (\(r_2^*\)): Substitute \(Q_2^* = 120\) into either curve: \[r_2^* = 2.0 + 0.02(120) = 2.0 + 2.4 = 4.4\% \quad (\Delta r^* = +0.6\text{ percentage points})\]
Measure Private Investment Crowded Out (\(\Delta I\)): \[\Delta I = I_2^* - I_1^* = \$120\text{B} - \$140\text{B} = -\$20\text{ billion}\]
Verify How the $50B Deficit Is Financed (Partial Crowding Out Decomposition): At \(r_2^* = 4.4\%\), private saving along \(Q_{S,0} = -50 + 50r\) rises to: \[S_{p,2} = -50 + 50(4.4) = -50 + 220 = \$170\text{ billion} \quad (\Delta S_p = +\$30\text{B})\] Thus, the \(\$50\text{B}\) deficit is financed by \(+\$30\text{B}\) in induced private saving plus \(-\$20\text{B}\) in crowded-out private investment (\(\Delta S_p + |\Delta I| = \$30\text{B} + \$20\text{B} = \$50\text{B}\)).

Set \(-20 + 40r_1^* = 220 - 20r_1^* \implies 60r_1^* = 240 \implies r_1^* = 4.0\%\) and \(I_1^* = 220 - 20(4.0) = \$140\text{ billion}\). (b) Shifted supply is \(Q_{S,1} = -50 + 40r\). Learning Outcomes
After completing this chapter, students should be able to:

Construct the aggregate consumption function (\(C = C_0 + cY_D\)) and saving schedule (\(S = -C_0 + (1-c)Y_D\)), and relate the marginal propensity to consume (\(MPC\)) to the marginal propensity to save (\(MPS\)).
Distinguish planned investment spending (\(I_{\text{planned}}\)) from unplanned inventory investment (\(I_{\text{unplanned}}\)) and explain how inventory adjustments drive short-run output toward equilibrium.
Identify short-run macroeconomic equilibrium on a 45-degree Keynesian cross diagram (\(Y^* = AE_{\text{planned}}\)) and solve for \(Y^*\) algebraically.
Calculate and compare the autonomous spending multiplier (\(k_G\)), the lump-sum tax multiplier (\(k_T\)), and the balanced-budget multiplier (\(k_{BB}\)).
Explain how proportional income taxes (\(t\)), marginal propensity to import (\(m\)), price-level changes, and interest-rate crowding out dampen the real-world multiplier.

Curriculum Alignment: Supports Course Learning Objectives MA-3 and C2002-2.


Key Terms
Autonomous consumption (\(C_0\)), disposable income (\(Y_D\)), marginal propensity to consume (\(MPC\)), marginal propensity to save (\(MPS\)), planned investment spending (\(I_{\text{planned}}\)), unplanned inventory investment (\(I_{\text{unplanned}}\)), planned aggregate expenditure (\(AE_{\text{planned}}\)), Keynesian cross, autonomous spending multiplier (\(k_G\)), lump-sum tax multiplier (\(k_T\)), balanced-budget multiplier (\(k_{BB}\)), and automatic stabilizers.






TipBring It Home: Why Does a $100 Billion Fiscal Package Move GDP by More—or Less—Than $100 Billion?



During an economic downturn, policymakers routinely debate two competing stimulus designs: direct government purchases of goods and infrastructure (\(\Delta G > 0\)) versus lump-sum tax rebates sent directly to households (\(\Delta T < 0\)). Because one person’s spending becomes another person’s income, an initial injection of spending triggers multiple rounds of induced household consumption. Yet households save part of any tax rebate rather than spending every dollar immediately, and leakages into taxes and imports shrink each successive round. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to prove algebraically and graphically why a $1 increase in government purchases raises equilibrium GDP by more than a $1 tax cut, and why a balanced-budget expansion (\(\Delta G = \Delta T\)) still expands short-run output.

title: 8  Chapter 8: Income, Expenditure, and the Keynesian Cross
section: 8.2 The Consumption Function, Saving Schedule, and Planned Investment
text:
8.2 The Consumption Function, Saving Schedule, and Planned Investment

Conceptual Introduction
Consumer spending (\(C\)) accounts for roughly two-thirds of total U.S. Gross Domestic Product, making household spending behavior the primary engine of short-run aggregate expenditure. Economists model aggregate consumption as a function of disposable income (\(Y_D = Y - T\)), the income households retain after paying net taxes (\(T\), defined as taxes minus government transfer payments). Even if a household’s current disposable income dropped to zero, it would still need to buy food, shelter, and utilities by drawing down past savings or borrowing; this baseline spending independent of current income is called autonomous consumption (\(C_0 > 0\)).
As disposable income rises, households increase their consumption, but by less than dollar-for-dollar because they allocate part of each additional dollar to saving. The fraction of an additional dollar of disposable income that households spend on consumption is the marginal propensity to consume (\(MPC = \Delta C / \Delta Y_D\)), while the fraction saved is the marginal propensity to save (\(MPS = \Delta S / \Delta Y_D\)). Because every extra dollar of disposable income must be either consumed or saved (\(\Delta Y_D = \Delta C + \Delta S\)), the two marginal propensities always sum to one: \(MPC + MPS = 1\).
Unlike consumer spending, which rises systematically with current disposable income, planned investment spending (\(I_{\text{planned}}\))—firms’ intended purchases of new machinery, commercial structures, software, and planned inventory additions—depends primarily on expected future profitability, capacity utilization, and the real interest rate. In the baseline Keynesian cross model, we treat planned investment (\(I_{\text{planned}}\)), government purchases (\(G\)), lump-sum taxes (\(T\)), and net exports (\(NX\)) as exogenous (autonomous) variables in the short run, allowing us to isolate how income-induced consumption drives macroeconomic equilibrium.


Visual Representation: The Aggregate Consumption Function
Figure 1 plots aggregate consumption (\(C\)) on the vertical axis against disposable income (\(Y_D\)) on the horizontal axis. The dashed \(45^\circ\) line represents all points where consumption equals disposable income (\(C = Y_D\), meaning household saving is zero).



Figure 1. The Aggregate Consumption Function and Saving Regions. The consumption line \(C = C_0 + cY_D\) has vertical intercept \(C_0\) and slope \(c = MPC < 1\). To the left of the break-even intersection with the \(45^\circ\) line, \(C > Y_D\) and households dis-save (\(S < 0\)); to the right, \(Y_D > C\) and household saving is positive (\(S = Y_D - C > 0\)).




Real-World Application: U.S. Disposable Income and Pandemic Stimulus Saving
Empirical data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) illustrate both the stability of the consumption function in normal times and how temporary shocks shift saving behavior. In 2020 and 2021, federal fiscal relief programs boosted real disposable personal income (FRED: ) while pandemic lockdowns restricted spending on in-person services. As a result, the U.S. personal saving rate (FRED: ) surged from roughly 7% in late 2019 to over 30% in April 2020, building more than $2 trillion in excess household savings. Once restrictions lifted in 2022–2024, households drew down those buffers, keeping real personal consumption expenditures (FRED: ) resilient even as interest rates rose.


Mathematical Foundation: Consumption and Saving Equations
Assuming a linear behavioral relationship, the aggregate consumption and saving functions are written as: \[\begin{align}
C &= C_0 + c\,Y_D = C_0 + c(Y - T), \qquad 0 < c < 1, \label{eq:ch8-consumption} \\
S_{\text{private}} &= Y_D - C = Y_D - \bigl(C_0 + c\,Y_D\bigr) = -C_0 + (1 - c)Y_D, \label{eq:ch8-saving}
\end{align}\] where \(c = MPC\) is the marginal propensity to consume and \(s = 1 - c = MPS\) is the marginal propensity to save.






TipWork It Out: Deriving Consumption and Saving Schedules



Suppose aggregate autonomous consumption is \(C_0 = \$100\text{ billion}\) and households spend \(80\%\) of each additional dollar of disposable income (\(c = MPC = 0.80\)).

Marginal Propensity to Save: \(MPS = 1 - MPC = 1 - 0.80 = 0.20\).
Consumption and Saving Functions:

\[
C = 100 + 0.80\,Y_D, \qquad S_{\text{private}} = -100 + 0.20\,Y_D.
\]

Break-Even Disposable Income (\(S_{\text{private}} = 0\)): Set \(C = Y_D\):

\[
Y_D = 100 + 0.80\,Y_D \implies 0.20\,Y_D = 100 \implies Y_D^{\text{break-even}} = \$500\text{ billion}.
\]

Evaluation at \(Y_D = \$1{,}250\text{ billion}\):

\[
C = 100 + 0.80(1{,}250) = 100 + 1{,}000 = \$1{,}100\text{ billion}, \qquad S_{\text{private}} = 1{,}250 - 1{,}100 = \$150\text{ billion}.
\]








NoteClear It Up: The Paradox of Thrift



For an individual household, increasing saving by cutting spending builds personal wealth. In a recessionary economy with sticky prices, however, if all households simultaneously try to save more by reducing autonomous consumption (\(C_0 \downarrow\)), aggregate expenditure falls, firms cut production, and national income (\(Y\)) contracts. Because saving also depends on income (\(S = -C_0 + sY_D\)), the resulting drop in \(Y\) can leave aggregate saving unchanged or even lower—a macroeconomic coordination failure John Maynard Keynes termed the paradox of thrift.

section: 8.3 Planned Aggregate Expenditure and the 45-Degree Keynesian Cross
text:
8.3 Planned Aggregate Expenditure and the 45-Degree Keynesian Cross

Conceptual Introduction
In the short run, many firms face menu costs, multi-quarter wage contracts, and sticky catalog prices. Rather than immediately slashing prices whenever weekly sales dip, firms adjust production quantities and manage buffer stocks of goods. Planned aggregate expenditure (\(AE_{\text{planned}}\)) is the total amount of spending that households, firms, the government, and foreign buyers plan to make on domestically produced final goods and services:
\[
AE_{\text{planned}} = C + I_{\text{planned}} + G + NX.
\]
Because firms produce output (\(Y\)) before knowing exact customer demand, actual total investment (\(I\)) equals planned investment plus unplanned inventory investment (\(I_{\text{unplanned}}\)):
\[
Y = C + I + G + NX = C + \bigl(I_{\text{planned}} + I_{\text{unplanned}}\bigr) + G + NX = AE_{\text{planned}} + I_{\text{unplanned}}.
\]
Rearranging this national accounting identity yields the fundamental adjustment law of the Keynesian cross:
\[
I_{\text{unplanned}} = Y - AE_{\text{planned}}.
\]
When real GDP exceeds planned spending (\(Y > AE_{\text{planned}}\)), unsold goods pile up in warehouses (\(I_{\text{unplanned}} > 0\)), prompting firms to cut factory orders and lay off workers until output falls back to \(Y^*\). Conversely, when planned spending exceeds current production (\(Y < AE_{\text{planned}}\)), shelves empty faster than anticipated (\(I_{\text{unplanned}} < 0\)), motivating firms to expand production and hire workers. Short-run macroeconomic equilibrium occurs exclusively at \(Y^*\), where actual output equals planned aggregate expenditure and unplanned inventory investment is zero (\(I_{\text{unplanned}} = 0\)).


Visual Representation: The 45-Degree Keynesian Cross
Figure 2 illustrates short-run equilibrium using the Keynesian cross. The \(45^\circ\) reference line maps all points where output equals planned expenditure (\(AE = Y\)), while the upward-sloping \(AE_{\text{planned}}\) line starts at autonomous expenditure \(A_0\) and rises with slope \(MPC\).



Figure 2. Short-Run Equilibrium in the 45-Degree Keynesian Cross. Equilibrium occurs at point \(E^*\), where \(AE_{\text{planned}} = 260 + 0.8Y\) intersects the \(45^\circ\) line at \(Y^* = \$1{,}300\text{ billion}\). Below \(Y^*\), \(AE_{\text{planned}} > Y\) causes unplanned inventory depletion (\(I_{\text{unplanned}} < 0\)), inducing firms to expand production; above \(Y^*\), \(Y > AE_{\text{planned}}\) causes unplanned inventory accumulation (\(I_{\text{unplanned}} > 0\)), inducing output cuts.




Real-World Application: Retail Inventory Overhangs and Production Adjustments
The inventory-adjustment mechanism is directly observable in quarterly National Income and Product Accounts (NIPA). Following supply-chain bottlenecks in 2021, major U.S. retailers over-ordered merchandise just as consumer demand rotated from physical goods back toward travel and dining. By mid-2022, bloated warehouse stocks—tracked in FRED series (Change in Private Inventories) alongside real GDP ()—forced retailers to slash new factory orders and discount existing stock. That inventory correction temporarily dragged down U.S. manufacturing output until inventory-to-sales ratios returned to equilibrium.


Mathematical Foundation: Solving for Equilibrium Output (\(Y^*\))
Substitute the behavioral consumption function \(C = C_0 + c(Y - T)\) and exogenous spending components (\(I_{\text{planned}}, G, NX\)) into \(AE_{\text{planned}}\):
\[
AE_{\text{planned}} = \underbrace{\bigl(C_0 - c\,T + I_{\text{planned}} + G + NX\bigr)}_{\text{Autonomous Expenditure } (A_0)} + c\,Y = A_0 + c\,Y.
\]
Setting \(Y = AE_{\text{planned}}\) and solving for equilibrium output \(Y^*\): \[\begin{align}
Y^* &= A_0 + c\,Y^* \nonumber \\
(1 - c)Y^* &= A_0 \nonumber \\
Y^* &= \frac{1}{1 - c}\,A_0 = \frac{1}{1 - c}\bigl(C_0 - c\,T + I_{\text{planned}} + G + NX\bigr). \label{eq:ch8-equilibrium}
\end{align}\]






TipWork It Out: Baseline Keynesian Cross Equilibrium and Inventory Table



Suppose a closed economy (\(NX = 0\)) has parameters in billions of dollars: \(C_0 = 100\), \(c = 0.8\), \(T = 50\), \(I_{\text{planned}} = 120\), and \(G = 80\).

Construct Planned Aggregate Expenditure:

\[
AE_{\text{planned}} = 100 + 0.8(Y - 50) + 120 + 80 = 100 + 0.8Y - 40 + 200 = 260 + 0.8Y.
\]
Here, autonomous aggregate expenditure is \(A_0 = \$260\text{ billion}\). * Solve for Short-Run Equilibrium Output (\(Y^*\)):
\[
Y^* = 260 + 0.8Y^* \implies 0.2Y^* = 260 \implies Y^* = \frac{260}{0.2} = \$1{,}300\text{ billion}.
\]

text:
8.4 The Autonomous Spending, Lump-Sum Tax, and Balanced-Budget Multipliers

Conceptual Introduction
When any component of autonomous expenditure (\(C_0\), \(I_{\text{planned}}\), \(G\), or \(NX\)) rises by \(\Delta A_0\), equilibrium real GDP increases by a multiple of that initial shock. Suppose the government purchases \(\Delta G = \$20\text{ billion}\) in new transit equipment. In Round 1, transit workers and suppliers earn \(\$20\text{ billion}\) in new income (\(\Delta Y_1 = \$20\text{ billion}\)). With \(MPC = 0.8\), those workers spend \(0.8 \times \$20\text{ billion} = \$16\text{ billion}\) on groceries, housing, and services in Round 2, generating \(\$16\text{ billion}\) of income for a second wave of producers, who in turn spend \(0.8 \times \$16\text{ billion} = \$12.8\text{ billion}\) in Round 3, and so on.
By contrast, consider a lump-sum tax cut of \(\Delta T = -\$20\text{ billion}\). In Round 1, government purchases do not rise directly; instead, households receive \(\$20\text{ billion}\) in extra disposable income. Because households save \(20\%\) (\(MPS = 0.2\)) and spend only \(80\%\) (\(MPC = 0.8\)), first-round aggregate expenditure rises by only \(-MPC \times \Delta T = -0.8(-\$20\text{ billion}) = +\$16\text{ billion}\) rather than \(+\$20\text{ billion}\). Consequently, the lump-sum tax multiplier (\(k_T\)) is smaller in absolute magnitude than the autonomous spending multiplier (\(k_G\)).
This asymmetry produces a remarkable corollary: if the government increases purchases by \(\Delta G = +\$20\text{ billion}\) and simultaneously finances the entire expenditure by raising lump-sum taxes by \(\Delta T = +\$20\text{ billion}\) (leaving the budget deficit unchanged), aggregate expenditure still increases on net. The \(+\$20\text{ billion}\) direct injection from \(\Delta G\) outweighs the \(-\$16\text{ billion}\) first-round consumption reduction from \(\Delta T\), yielding a net expansion of \(\Delta Y^* = +\$20\text{ billion}\)—meaning the balanced-budget multiplier (\(k_{BB}\)) equals exactly \(1.0\) in the baseline lump-sum tax model.


Visual Representation: Multiplier Shift in the Keynesian Cross
Figure 3 shows how an autonomous spending increase of \(\Delta G = \$20\text{ billion}\) shifts the \(AE_{\text{planned}}\) schedule vertically upward from \(AE_1 = 260 + 0.8Y\) to \(AE_2 = 280 + 0.8Y\), moving equilibrium along the \(45^\circ\) line from \(E_1^*\) (\(Y_1^* = \$1{,}300\text{ billion}\)) to \(E_2^*\) (\(Y_2^* = \$1{,}400\text{ billion}\)).



Figure 3. The Autonomous Spending Multiplier in the Keynesian Cross. An autonomous increase in government purchases of \(\Delta G = \$20\text{ billion}\) shifts the expenditure line vertically upward by \(\$20\text{ billion}\). Because \(MPC = 0.8\), induced consumption rounds amplify the shock by \(k_G = 1/(1 - 0.8) = 5\), raising equilibrium output by \(\Delta Y^* = \$100\text{ billion}\) (from \(\$1{,}300\text{ billion}\) to \(\$1{,}400\text{ billion}\)).




Real-World Application: Direct Infrastructure Spending vs. Lump-Sum Tax Rebates
When Congress designed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 and the 2020–2021 fiscal relief packages, economists at the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) explicitly applied differential multipliers across policy instruments. Direct federal purchases and infrastructure grants (\(\Delta G\)) entered aggregate expenditure immediately at \(100\%\) of their dollar value, whereas one-time lump-sum tax rebates (\(\Delta T < 0\)) had lower first-round bang-for-the-buck because households saved a substantial portion—or used rebates to pay down credit card balances—rather than spending the full transfer immediately.


Mathematical Foundation: Comparing the Three Baseline Multipliers
Taking first differences of Equation~\(\eqref{eq:ch8-equilibrium}\) while holding \(c\) constant yields the three canonical multipliers of the baseline closed economy: \[\begin{align}
k_G &= \frac{\Delta Y^*}{\Delta G} = \frac{1}{1 - c} = \frac{1}{MPS}, \label{eq:ch8-kg} \\
k_T &= \frac{\Delta Y^*}{\Delta T} = \frac{-c}{1 - c} = -\frac{MPC}{MPS}, \label{eq:ch8-kt} \\
k_{BB} &= k_G + k_T = \frac{1}{1 - c} + \frac{-c}{1 - c} = \frac{1 - c}{1 - c} = 1. \label{eq:ch8-kbb}
\end{align}\]






TipWork It Out: Calculating \(\Delta Y^*\) Under Three Fiscal Policies



Continue with the baseline economy from Section 3 (\(C_0 = 100\), \(c = 0.8\), \(T = 50\), \(I_{\text{planned}} = 120\), \(G = 80\), initial \(Y_1^* = \$1{,}300\text{ billion}\)):

Policy A — Autonomous Government Purchases Increase (\(\Delta G = +\$20\text{ billion}\)):

\[
k_G = \frac{1}{1 - 0.8} = \frac{1}{0.2} = 5.0 \implies \Delta Y^* = 5.0 \times (+\$20\text{ billion}) = +\$100\text{ billion}.
\]
New equilibrium output is \(Y_2^* = 1{,}300 + 100 = \$1{,}400\text{ billion}\). * Policy B — Lump-Sum Tax Cut (\(\Delta T = -\$20\text{ billion}\), holding \(G = 80\)):
\[
k_T = \frac{-0.8}{1 - 0.8} = \frac{-0.8}{0.2} = -4.0 \implies \Delta Y^* = (-4.0) \times (-\$20\text{ billion}) = +\$80\text{ billion}.
\]
New equilibrium output is \(Y_2^* = 1{,}300 + 80 = \$1{,}380\text{ billion}\)—\(\$20\text{ billion}\) less than under Policy A because households save \(0.2 \times \$20\text{ billion} = \$4\text{ billion}\) of the tax cut in Round 1. * Policy C — Balanced-Budget Expansion (\(\Delta G = +\$20\text{ billion}\) and \(\Delta T = +\$20\text{ billion}\)):
\[
\Delta Y^* = k_G\,\Delta G + k_T\,\Delta T = 5.0(20) + (-4.0)(20) = 100 - 80 = +\$20\text{ billion}.
\]
Equilibrium output rises by exactly the size of the balanced-budget expansion (\(Y_2^* = \$1{,}320\text{ billion}\)), confirming \(k_{BB} = 1.0\).








Note[Advanced: For Economics Majors] Infinite Geometric Series and Comparative Statics



The autonomous spending multiplier is the sum of an infinite geometric series of induced consumption rounds. For an autonomous injection \(\Delta A_0\) and constant marginal propensity to consume \(c \in (0,1)\):
\[
\Delta Y^* = \Delta A_0 + c\,\Delta A_0 + c^2\,\Delta A_0 + c^3\,\Delta A_0 + \cdots = \Delta A_0 \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c^n = \frac{1}{1 - c}\,\Delta A_0.
\]
Equivalently, applying implicit differentiation to \(Y^* = C_0 + c(Y^* - T) + I_{\text{planned}} + G + NX\) yields the exact comparative-static partial derivatives:
\[
\frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial G} = \frac{1}{1 - c} > 0, \qquad \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial T} = \frac{-c}{1 - c} < 0, \qquad \left.\frac{dY^*}{dG}\right|_{dT = dG} = \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial G} + \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial T} = 1.
\]

8.5 Leakages, Automatic Stabilizers, and Real-World Multiplier Dampeners

Conceptual Introduction
In our simplified baseline model (\(k_G = 1/(1 - c)\)), private saving was the only leakage from the domestic spending stream. In modern open economies, two additional income-sensitive leakages siphon purchasing power out of each spending round: proportional income taxes (\(T = T_0 + tY\), where \(t\) is the marginal income tax rate) and induced imports (\(IM = IM_0 + mY\), where \(m\) is the marginal propensity to import). Every additional dollar of national income (\(Y\)) now generates less than \(c\) dollars of domestic spending because households pay \(t\) in taxes before consuming out of after-tax income, and spend \(m\) on foreign-produced goods rather than domestic output.
Because proportional taxes and imports reduce the slope of the \(AE_{\text{planned}}\) line from \(c\) to \(c(1 - t) - m\), they flatten the expenditure schedule and shrink the expenditure multiplier. While a smaller multiplier reduces the potency of discretionary stimulus, it simultaneously acts as an automatic stabilizer: when a recession hits and national income falls, tax liabilities automatically drop and import spending falls, cushioning disposable income and preventing a steep downward spiral without requiring new legislation from Congress.
Beyond tax and import leakages, three macroeconomic channels further dampen the real-world multiplier compared to the fixed-price Keynesian cross benchmark: (1) rising aggregate demand pushes up the aggregate price level when the economy nears full capacity, eroding real purchasing power; (2) higher nominal income increases money demand and interest rates, partially crowding out interest-sensitive private investment; and (3) households often smooth consumption based on permanent income rather than reacting solely to temporary income fluctuations.


Visual Representation: How Leakages Flatten the Expenditure Line
Figure 4 compares the steep simple \(AE_{\text{planned}}\) curve (slope \(c = 0.8\), multiplier \(k = 5.0\)) against a flatter open-economy \(AE_{\text{planned}}\) curve incorporating proportional taxes (\(t = 0.25\)) and imports (\(m = 0.10\)), where the marginal propensity to spend on domestic output falls to \(c(1 - t) - m = 0.50\) and the multiplier drops to \(k = 2.0\).



Figure 4. Tax and Import Leakages Flatten the Expenditure Schedule. Incorporating proportional income taxes (\(t\)) and induced imports (\(m\)) lowers the slope of \(AE_{\text{planned}}\) from \(c\) to \(c(1-t)-m\). A flatter expenditure line shrinks the multiplier from \(5.0\) to \(2.0\), automatically dampening cyclical output volatility.




Real-World Application: U.S. Automatic Stabilizers in Recessions
In the U.S. federal budget, progressive personal income taxes, corporate profit taxes, and state–federal Unemployment Insurance (UI) operate automatically without waiting for Congressional votes. During economic contractions—such as the 2008–2009 Great Recession and the 2020 COVID-19 downturn—federal tax receipts fell automatically while UI benefit outlays (tracked in FRED series and reflected in total government net saving ) rose immediately as layoffs occurred. These built-in stabilizers offset roughly 15% to 25% of initial GDP shocks before any discretionary stimulus bill was signed.






TipFRED Data: Realized GDP Is Not Planned Expenditure



FRED series reports quarterly U.S. real Gross Domestic Product in billions of chained 2017 dollars at a seasonally adjusted annual rate. Because measures realized output (\(Y = AE_{\text{planned}} + I_{\text{unplanned}}\)), a raw quarter-to-quarter change in reflects both planned spending shifts and unintended inventory swings, as well as simultaneous changes in interest rates, prices, and expectations. Empirical macroeconomists therefore identify fiscal multipliers using plausibly exogenous policy shocks—such as military procurement shifts or state-level formula grants—rather than dividing \(\Delta\texttt{GDPC1}\) by raw budget changes.




Mathematical Foundation: The Open-Economy Tax-Damped Multiplier
Let net taxes be \(T = T_0 + t\,Y\) and imports be \(IM = IM_0 + m\,Y\), while exports remain exogenous (\(EX = EX_0\)). Planned aggregate expenditure becomes: \[\begin{align}
AE_{\text{planned}} &= C_0 + c(Y - T_0 - t\,Y) + I_{\text{planned}} + G + EX_0 - (IM_0 + m\,Y) \nonumber \\
&= \underbrace{\bigl(C_0 - c\,T_0 + I_{\text{planned}} + G + EX_0 - IM_0\bigr)}_{\text{Autonomous Expenditure } (A_0)} + \bigl[c(1 - t) - m\bigr]Y.
\end{align}\] Setting \(Y^* = AE_{\text{planned}}\) and solving for \(Y^*\) gives the leakage-damped multiplier:
\[
Y^* = \frac{1}{1 - c(1 - t) + m}\,A_0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad k_{\text{damped}} = \frac{1}{1 - c(1 - t) + m}. \label{eq:ch8-damped-multiplier}
\]






TipWork It Out: Quantifying the Multiplier with Taxes and Imports



Suppose \(c = 0.80\), the marginal income tax rate is \(t = 0.25\), and the marginal propensity to import is \(m = 0.10\).

Compute the Domestic Marginal Propensity to Spend:

\[
c(1 - t) - m = 0.80(1 - 0.25) - 0.10 = 0.80(0.75) - 0.10 = 0.60 - 0.10 = 0.50.
\]
Out of every additional \(\$1.00\) of national income, \(\$0.25\) goes to taxes, \(\$0.15\) goes to private saving (\(0.20 \times \$0.75\)), and \(\$0.10\) goes to imports—leaving \(\$0.50\) of induced domestic spending. * Compute the Leakage-Damped Multiplier:
\[
k_{\text{damped}} = \frac{1}{1 - 0.50} = \frac{1}{0.50} = 2.0.
\]

Output Impact of \(\Delta G = +\$20\text{ billion}\):

\[
\Delta Y^* = 2.0 \times (+\$20\text{ billion}) = +\$40\text{ billion},
\]
compared to \(+\$100\text{ billion}\) in the closed-economy lump-sum tax benchmark.








NoteClear It Up: A Multiplier Is Conditional, Not a Universal Constant



The algebraic multiplier depends strictly on model assumptions regarding sticky prices, idle productive capacity, tax structures, trade openness, and central bank interest-rate responses. During a deep recession with high unemployment and near-zero interest rates, multipliers tend to be larger; near full employment, supply bottlenecks and higher interest rates crowd out private spending, pushing the effective multiplier closer to zero.

8.6 Chapter Summary and Check Your Understanding






TipBring It Home: Designing Effective Stabilization Policy



Returning to our opening policy dilemma: the Keynesian cross demonstrates that fiscal policy operates through a chain of income-induced consumption rounds, making direct government purchases (\(k_G = \frac{1}{1-c}\)) more potent dollar-for-dollar than lump-sum tax cuts (\(k_T = \frac{-c}{1-c}\)) because households save a fraction of tax rebates immediately. Even a balanced-budget expansion (\(\Delta G = \Delta T\)) expands short-run output with a multiplier of \(1.0\). In real-world economies, however, proportional income taxes, import leakages, rising prices, and interest-rate crowding out dampen the multiplier—while simultaneously serving as automatic stabilizers that cushion recessions without legislative delay.



Check Your Understanding

(Conceptual — Inventory Adjustment) Suppose real GDP is currently \(\$1{,}500\text{ billion}\) while planned aggregate expenditure is \(\$1{,}420\text{ billion}\). Calculate unplanned inventory investment (\(I_{\text{unplanned}}\)) and explain how firms will adjust production over the coming quarters.
(Analytical — Consumption and Saving) If aggregate autonomous consumption is \(C_0 = \$120\text{ billion}\) and \(MPS = 0.25\), write the consumption and saving functions in terms of disposable income (\(Y_D\)), and find the break-even level of disposable income where \(S_{\text{private}} = 0\).
(Numerical — Comparing Fiscal Multipliers) In a closed economy with lump-sum taxes and \(MPC = 0.75\):
Calculate the autonomous government-purchases multiplier (\(k_G\)) and the lump-sum tax multiplier (\(k_T\)).
Compare the change in equilibrium GDP (\(\Delta Y^*\)) from a \(\$40\text{ billion}\) increase in \(G\) versus a \(\$40\text{ billion}\) cut in \(T\).
What is \(\Delta Y^*\) if the government increases \(G\) by \(\$40\text{ billion}\) and raises lump-sum taxes \(T\) by \(\$40\text{ billion}\) simultaneously?
(Open-Economy Application — Leakage-Damped Multiplier) Suppose \(c = 0.75\), the marginal income tax rate is \(t = 0.20\), and the marginal propensity to import is \(m = 0.10\). Calculate the leakage-damped multiplier and determine how much equilibrium GDP rises when exports increase autonomously by \(\Delta EX_0 = +\$30\text{ billion}\).



Solutions to Check Your Understanding

\(I_{\text{unplanned}} = Y - AE_{\text{planned}} = 1{,}500 - 1{,}420 = +\$80\text{ billion}\). Because production exceeds planned sales, unsold goods accumulate in inventories, prompting firms to cut orders and reduce output until \(Y\) falls to \(Y^*\).
Since \(MPC = 1 - MPS = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75\), the functions are \(C = 120 + 0.75\,Y_D\) and \(S_{\text{private}} = -120 + 0.25\,Y_D\). Setting \(S_{\text{private}} = 0\) gives \(0.25\,Y_D = 120 \implies Y_D^{\text{break-even}} = \$480\text{ billion}\).
With \(MPC = 0.75\) and \(MPS = 0.25\):
\(k_G = \frac{1}{1 - 0.75} = 4.0\), and \(k_T = \frac{-0.75}{1 - 0.75} = -3.0\).
For \(\Delta G = +\$40\text{ billion}\): \(\Delta Y^* = 4.0 \times 40 = +\$160\text{ billion}\). For \(\Delta T = -\$40\text{ billion}\): \(\Delta Y^* = (-3.0) \times (-40) = +\$120\text{ billion}\).
For \(\Delta G = \Delta T = +\$40\text{ billion}\): \(\Delta Y^* = 160 - 120 = +\$40\text{ billion}\) (\(k_{BB} = 1.0\)).
The domestic marginal propensity to spend is \(c(1 - t) - m = 0.75(1 - 0.20) - 0.10 = 0.60 - 0.10 = 0.50\). Thus \(k_{\text{damped}} = \frac{1}{1 - 0.50} = 2.0\), and an autonomous export increase of \(\Delta EX_0 = +\$30\text{ billion}\) raises equilibrium output by \(\Delta Y^* = 2.0 \times 30 = +\$60\text{ billion}\).

TipBring It Home: Why Did 2021–2023 Combine High Inflation with Shifting Output?



In 2020, pandemic lockdowns caused total spending and production to plunge simultaneously. By 2021–2022, aggressive fiscal stimulus and pent-up household demand collided with global semiconductor shortages, port bottlenecks, and a sharp spike in global energy prices following geopolitical conflict. Consumer price inflation () surged to a four-decade high above 9%, while policymakers debated whether rising prices reflected excessive aggregate demand or constrained aggregate supply. The \(AD\text{–}AS\) model provides the exact analytical lens required to separate demand-driven expansions from supply-driven stagflation.

text:
9.2 Aggregate Demand: Total Planned Spending and the Price Level

Conceptual Introduction
Aggregate Demand (\(AD\)) represents the total quantity of domestically produced final goods and services that households, firms, governments, and foreign buyers plan to purchase at each aggregate price level (\(P\)), holding all non-price determinants constant (ceteris paribus). Summing across the four expenditure sectors established in Chapter 4 gives total planned spending:
\[
AD = C + I + G + NX
\]
Unlike a microeconomic demand curve—which holds all other prices and consumer income constant while varying the relative price of a single good—the \(AD\) curve tracks economy-wide real output (\(Y\)) as the overall price level (\(P\), measured by the GDP deflator or CPI) changes across all markets simultaneously.
Three distinct macroeconomic channels explain why the \(AD\) curve slopes downward from left to right:

The Wealth (Real-Balances) Effect: When the aggregate price level \(P\) falls, the real purchasing power of households’ fixed nominal financial assets (cash, checking deposits, nominal bonds) rises. Feeling wealthier, households increase real consumption spending (\(C\)).
The Interest-Rate Effect: A lower price level reduces the amount of money households and firms need to hold for everyday transactions. As money demand falls, nominal and real interest rates (\(r\)) decline, lowering borrowing costs and stimulating business investment (\(I\)) and durable consumption (\(C\)).
The Exchange-Rate (Net Export) Effect: When lower domestic interest rates reduce the return on U.S. financial assets relative to foreign assets, capital outflows depreciate the domestic currency. A weaker currency makes domestic exports cheaper for foreign buyers and imports more expensive for domestic residents, increasing net exports (\(NX = X - M\)).

When any factor other than the current domestic price level alters planned spending at every price level, the entire \(AD\) curve shifts. Rightward shifts (\(AD_1 \rightarrow AD_2\)) result from stronger consumer confidence, higher expected business profitability, expansionary fiscal policy (higher \(G\) or lower taxes \(T\)), expansionary monetary policy (lower policy interest rates), faster foreign GDP growth, or currency depreciation. Leftward shifts occur when these forces reverse.


Visual Representation



Figure 1. Reading the \(AD\) Curve: A lower price level (\(P_A \rightarrow P_B\)) induces a movement along \(AD_1\) from point \(A\) to point \(B\) (\(Y_A \rightarrow Y_B\)), whereas an autonomous spending surge at constant price level \(P_B\) shifts the entire curve rightward from \(AD_1\) to \(AD_2\) (point \(B\) to point \(C\)).








NoteClear It Up: Movement Along \(AD\) vs. Shift of \(AD\)



A change in the domestic aggregate price level \(P\) causes a movement along a stationary \(AD\) curve via the wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate effects. By contrast, a change in autonomous consumption, investment, government purchases, net exports, or monetary/fiscal policy at any given price level shifts the entire \(AD\) curve. Never treat an endogenous change in \(P\) as a shifter of \(AD\).




Mathematical Foundation
Assume linear aggregate planned expenditure where autonomous spending responds inversely to the price level \(P\) (capturing the wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate channels with slope parameter \(\beta > 0\)):
\[
AD: \quad Y = A_0 - \beta P \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad P = \frac{A_0}{\beta} - \frac{1}{\beta} Y
\]
Here, \(A_0\) summarizes non-price autonomous spending determinants (\(C_0, I_0, G, NX_0\)). Any increase \(\Delta A_0 > 0\) shifts the horizontal intercept rightward by \(\Delta Y = \Delta A_0\) at every price level \(P\).






TipWork It Out: Quantifying a Movement Along \(AD\) vs. a Fiscal Shift



Suppose baseline Aggregate Demand is given by \(Y = 45 - 0.25P\) (with \(Y\) in trillions of 2017 dollars and \(P\) as a price index).

Movement Along \(AD\): Calculate real output demanded when \(P = 120\) versus \(P = 100\).
At \(P = 120\): \(Y_A = 45 - 0.25(120) = 45 - 30 = \$15.0\text{ trillion}\).
At \(P = 100\): \(Y_B = 45 - 0.25(100) = 45 - 25 = \$20.0\text{ trillion}\).
Moving from \(P = 120\) to \(P = 100\) expands quantity demanded by \(+\$5.0\text{ trillion}\) along the same curve.
Shift of \(AD\): Suppose an autonomous investment boom increases \(A_0\) by \(\$4.0\text{ trillion}\) at every price level, yielding \(Y = 49 - 0.25P\). At \(P = 100\):

\[
Y_C = 49 - 0.25(100) = 49 - 25 = \$24.0\text{ trillion}
\]
At an unchanged price level of \(P = 100\), the \(AD\) curve shifts horizontally rightward by \(\Delta Y = \$4.0\text{ trillion}\).




Real-World Application
Interest-Rate Sensitivity in U.S. Residential Investment (2022–2024): When the Federal Reserve raised its administered interest-rate corridor during 2022–2023 to curb post-pandemic inflation, 30-year fixed mortgage rates rose from roughly 3% to over 7%. Even before overall consumer prices fell, higher borrowing costs sharply reduced planned residential investment (\(I\)) and auto/durable purchases (\(C\)), shifting the U.S. \(AD\) curve leftward relative to its 2021 trajectory and cooling excess demand.

section: 9.3 Short-Run and Long-Run Aggregate Supply
text:
9.3 Short-Run and Long-Run Aggregate Supply

Conceptual Introduction
Aggregate Supply links the aggregate price level (\(P\)) to the total quantity of real goods and services (\(Y\)) that domestic firms are willing and able to produce. Crucially, supply behavior depends on the time horizon over which input costs adjust:

Short-Run Aggregate Supply (\(SRAS\)): In the short run, nominal wages and many input prices are sticky—locked in by multi-year union contracts, annual salary cycles, or menu costs. When the overall price level \(P\) rises while nominal unit production costs remain temporarily fixed, revenue per unit rises faster than cost per unit. Profit margins widen, inducing firms to expand production and hire more workers, which gives \(SRAS\) its positive upward slope.
Long-Run Aggregate Supply (\(LRAS\)): In the long run, all nominal wages, input prices, and price expectations adjust fully to match the aggregate price level. Because doubling all output prices and all input wages leaves real relative prices and profit margins unchanged, long-run output is independent of \(P\). Consequently, \(LRAS\) is vertical at potential output (\(Y^*\))—the sustainable level of real GDP determined by the economy’s labor force, physical and human capital stock, natural resources, technology, and institutions (corresponding to the natural rate of unemployment \(u^*\)).

While \(LRAS\) shifts rightward over decades through capital deepening, labor force growth, and technological innovation (mirroring outward shifts of the Macroeconomic PPF in Chapter 2), \(SRAS\) shifts whenever unit production costs or price expectations change:

Nominal Wage Changes: Higher nominal wage settlements raise unit labor costs and shift \(SRAS\) leftward (upward).
Commodity and Energy Prices: Spikes in oil, electricity, or raw material prices raise production costs and shift \(SRAS\) leftward.
Expected Price Level (\(P^e\)): When workers and firms expect higher inflation (\(P^e \uparrow\)), they negotiate higher nominal wages today, shifting \(SRAS\) leftward.
Productivity Shocks: Advances in total factor productivity lower unit costs and shift both \(SRAS\) and \(LRAS\) rightward.



Visual Representation



Figure 2. Macroeconomic Equilibrium and Output Gaps: Long-run equilibrium occurs at \(E^*\) where \(AD_1\), \(SRAS_1\), and vertical \(LRAS\) intersect at \((Y^*, P^*)\). Short-run equilibria to the left of \(Y^*\) create recessionary gaps (\(u > u^*\)), whereas equilibria to the right of \(Y^*\) create inflationary gaps (\(u < u^*\)).








NoteClear It Up: Why Does \(SRAS\) Slope Upward While \(LRAS\) Is Vertical?



A higher aggregate price level boosts production only when output prices rise faster than nominal wages and input costs. In the short run, sticky contracts hold nominal wages temporarily fixed, so higher \(P\) raises profit per unit and expands real GDP along \(SRAS\). In the long run, nominal wages adjust proportionally with \(P\), restoring original real wages and profit margins; therefore, long-run output returns to potential GDP (\(Y^*\)) regardless of the price level.




Mathematical Foundation
In linear form, Short-Run Aggregate Supply reflects sticky nominal wages (\(W_0\)) anchored to the expected price level (\(P^e\)) with supply slope parameter \(\gamma > 0\):
\[
SRAS: \quad Y = Y^* + \gamma (P - P^e) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad P = P^e + \frac{1}{\gamma}(Y - Y^*)
\]
When actual prices equal expected prices (\(P = P^e\)), short-run output equals potential output (\(Y = Y^*\)), which defines the vertical \(LRAS\) schedule. If \(P > P^e\), real wages (\(W_0 / P\)) fall temporarily and firms expand output above \(Y^*\); if \(P < P^e\), real wages rise and firms cut production below \(Y^*\).


Real-World Application
AI Infrastructure, Productivity, and \(LRAS\) vs. \(SRAS\): Heavy capital investment in data centers, automation, and cloud computing initially boosts \(AD\) through higher business investment (\(I\)). Over a multi-year horizon, however, if those technologies raise output per worker across logistics, healthcare, and software, they reduce unit labor costs—shifting both \(SRAS\) and vertical \(LRAS\) rightward and allowing higher non-inflationary potential output (\(Y^*\)).

section: 9.4 Demand Shocks, Stagflation, and Long-Run Adjustment
text:
9.4 Demand Shocks, Stagflation, and Long-Run Adjustment

Conceptual Introduction
Macroeconomic fluctuations arise from exogenous shocks that displace the economy from \(E^* = (Y^*, P^*)\):

Positive Demand Shock (\(AD_1 \rightarrow AD_2\)) and Self-Correction: A surge in planned spending raises both short-run output (\(Y_2 > Y^*\)) and the price level (\(P_2 > P^*\)), opening an inflationary gap where unemployment falls below \(u^*\). Because labor markets are tight and workers’ real purchasing power has been eroded by higher prices (\(P_2 > P^e\)), workers demand higher nominal wages as contracts renew. Rising nominal wages increase unit production costs, shifting \(SRAS\) leftward (\(SRAS_1 \rightarrow SRAS_2\)) until output returns to \(Y^*\) at a permanently higher price level (\(P_3 > P_2\)). Conversely, after a negative demand shock creates a recessionary gap (\(Y < Y^*\)), high unemployment eventually puts downward pressure on nominal wage growth, shifting \(SRAS\) rightward back to \(Y^*\)—though downward nominal wage stickiness often makes self-correction from recessions slow and painful.
Adverse Supply Shock (\(SRAS_1 \rightarrow SRAS_2\)) and Stagflation: A sharp spike in energy or commodity costs shifts \(SRAS\) leftward. In the short run, real output falls (\(Y_2 < Y^*\), raising unemployment) while the price level rises (\(P_2 > P^*\)). This combination of economic stagnation and rising inflation is called stagflation. Unlike demand shocks—where output and prices move in the same direction—supply shocks push output and prices in opposite directions, creating a painful policy dilemma because stimulating \(AD\) fights unemployment at the cost of even higher inflation.



Visual Representation



Figure 3. Comparing Demand and Supply Shocks: In Panel A, a positive demand shock moves the economy from \(E_1\) to \(E_2\) (\(Y_2 > Y^*\), \(P_2 > P_1\)), followed by rising nominal wages shifting \(SRAS_1 \rightarrow SRAS_2\) to long-run equilibrium \(E_3\) at \(Y^*\). In Panel B, an adverse supply shock shifts \(SRAS_1 \rightarrow SRAS_2\), reducing output (\(Y_2 < Y^*\)) while raising the price level (\(P_2 > P_1\)).




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra-First with Optional Calculus Box)






TipWork It Out: Complete Equilibrium, Demand Shock, Self-Correction, and Stagflation



Consider an economy described by the following linear schedules (\(Y\) in trillions of chained 2017 dollars, \(P\) as price index):
\[
AD_1: \; P = 180 - 4Y \qquad\qquad SRAS_1: \; P = 20 + 4Y \qquad\qquad LRAS: \; Y^* = 20
\]
Part A: Initial Long-Run Equilibrium (\(E_1\)) \ Set \(AD_1 = SRAS_1\):
\[
180 - 4Y = 20 + 4Y \implies 160 = 8Y \implies Y_1 = 20
\]
Substitute \(Y_1 = 20\) into \(AD_1\): \(P_1 = 180 - 4(20) = 100\). Since \(Y_1 = Y^* = 20\), the economy begins in long-run equilibrium at \((Y^* = 20, P_1 = 100)\).
Part B: Positive Demand Shock (\(AD_1 \rightarrow AD_2\)) and Output Gap \ Suppose a surge in business investment shifts \(AD\) to \(AD_2: \; P = 196 - 4Y\). Equate \(AD_2 = SRAS_1\):
\[
196 - 4Y = 20 + 4Y \implies 176 = 8Y \implies Y_2 = 22
\]
Substitute \(Y_2 = 22\) into \(AD_2\): \(P_2 = 196 - 4(22) = 108\). \ The economy experiences an inflationary gap of \(Y_2 - Y^* = 22 - 20 = +\$2.0\text{ trillion}\) (\(+10\%\) above potential), and the price level rises by \(8\%\).
Part C: Long-Run Self-Correction (\(SRAS_1 \rightarrow SRAS_2\)) \ Tight labor markets bid up nominal wages until output returns to \(Y_3 = Y^* = 20\) along \(AD_2\):
\[
P_3 = 196 - 4(20) = 116
\]
The new short-run supply curve shifts upward by \(\Delta P = +16\) to \(SRAS_2: \; P = 36 + 4Y\). In the long run, real output returns to \(Y^* = 20\) while the price level settles permanently at \(P_3 = 116\).
Part D: Adverse Supply Shock / Stagflation (\(SRAS_1 \rightarrow SRAS_{\text{shock}}\)) \ Return to initial equilibrium \(E_1 = (20, 100)\) on \(AD_1\) (\(P = 180 - 4Y\)). Suppose an energy price spike shifts short-run supply upward by \(16\) index points to \(SRAS_{\text{shock}}: \; P = 36 + 4Y\). Equate \(AD_1 = SRAS_{\text{shock}}\):
\[
180 - 4Y = 36 + 4Y \implies 144 = 8Y \implies Y_{\text{stag}} = 18
\]
Substitute \(Y_{\text{stag}} = 18\) into \(AD_1\): \(P_{\text{stag}} = 180 - 4(18) = 108\). \ Output falls by \(\$2.0\text{ trillion}\) (a recessionary gap of \(-\$2.0\text{ trillion}\)) while the price level simultaneously rises from \(100\) to \(108\).








NoteOptional Advanced Extension: Comparative Statics via Total Differentiation



For quantitative economics majors, consider a general differentiable short-run system:
\[
AD: \; Y = D(P, G) \quad (D_P < 0, \; D_G > 0) \qquad\text{and}\qquad SRAS: \; P = S(Y, W_0) \quad (S_Y > 0, \; S_{W_0} > 0)
\]
Taking total differentials holding nominal wages \(W_0\) fixed (\(dW_0 = 0\)) in the short run:
\[
dY = D_P \, dP + D_G \, dG \qquad\text{and}\qquad dP = S_Y \, dY
\]
Substituting \(dP = S_Y \, dY\) into the \(AD\) differential yields the short-run fiscal output and price multipliers:
\[
\frac{dY}{dG} = \frac{D_G}{1 - D_P S_Y} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{dP}{dG} = \frac{S_Y D_G}{1 - D_P S_Y}
\]
Because \(D_P < 0\) and \(S_Y > 0\), the denominator \(1 - D_P S_Y > 1\). Thus, an upward-sloping \(SRAS\) curve (\(S_Y > 0\)) dampens the short-run output multiplier relative to the fixed-price Keynesian Cross (\(S_Y = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{dY}{dG} = D_G\)) by crowding out price-sensitive spending as \(P\) rises. In the long run, as \(S_Y \rightarrow \infty\) along vertical \(LRAS\), \(\lim_{S_Y \to \infty} \frac{dY}{dG} = 0\) and \(\lim_{S_Y \to \infty} \frac{dP}{dG} = -\frac{D_G}{D_P} > 0\).




Real-World Application






TipFRED Data Diagnostics: Identifying Shocks Across \texttt{GDPC1



, , and } Macroeconomists track three canonical St. Louis Fed FRED series to diagnose historical episodes:

: Real Gross Domestic Product (billions of chained 2017 dollars, quarterly, seasonally adjusted annual rate).
: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items (index \(1982\text{–}1984 = 100\), monthly, seasonally adjusted).
: Civilian Unemployment Rate (percent, monthly, seasonally adjusted).

Empirical Identification Rule: During the 2008–2009 Great Recession, contracted while decelerated/dipped and surged toward 10%—the classic signature of an adverse demand shock. Conversely, during the 1973–1975 and 1979–1980 oil price shocks, fell and jumped while inflation exceeded 11%—the unmistakable empirical footprint of an adverse supply shock (stagflation). Because monthly price series () and quarterly output series () differ in frequency and undergo statistical revisions, structural identification requires examining relative input prices alongside aggregate movements.








TipBring It Home: Resolving the 2021–2023 Inflation Puzzle



Applying the \(AD\text{–}AS\) framework reveals that 2021–2023 combined both shocks simultaneously: expansionary demand shifted \(AD\) rightward (pushing output up and unemployment down toward 3.4%), while supply-chain bottlenecks and energy spikes shifted \(SRAS\) leftward. Both shifts pushed the price level \(P\) upward in the same direction, explaining why inflation surged dramatically even as real GDP recovery moderated.
